rounds.evidence_text: On a night when the roar of go-karts was silenced by a nefarious deed, Detective Winston finds himself investigating the peculiar murder of Gary, slain by a rarely-seen sai with two unlikely suspects: Frederick and Jerome.
Detective Winston flicked through the reports once again. The guy is a dock worker, moved shipping containers around all day. It was a harmless hobby, but it didn't sit right.
"The dock's a rough place, Winston," said Officer Daniels, a baby-faced officer with a knack of not following orders, "You can't be weak and thrive there."

"I bet Frederick's co-workers would tell you about his strength and dexterity. Cargo isn't a walk in the park," Winston said, taking in Daniels' recommendation. Strength and dexterity... it reminded him of something. The weapon, a sai, was found in Frederick's collection.
Winston rubbed his brow lightly and continued turning the pages. Frederick was a devotee of warfare artifacts. From ancient katana to modern assault rifles, Frederick had them all.

"Frederick goes for racing during his free time," the report read. In fact, suspicious activity at the go-kart track was often reported around Frederick's usual racing time. Winston remembered Frederick's racing schedule: every Thursday at six, without fail.

On the day Gary was killed, Frederick and Gary were both at the go-kart track. Gary, a joker at heart, was seen messing around with Frederick's go-kart, the very same one that Frederick had previously confronted others about.
Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair. Daniels had a defensive glance in his eye.
"But he's just an enthusiast! And skilled, I heard," Daniels defended, almost pleadingly.
Winston only nodded, his mind already spinning with strategies and weak alibis.
"He's also a dockworker, known for his strength and dexterity, able to handle heavy cargo safely." He paused. "Isn't a sai a pretty lightweight weapon?"
"Yes sir." Daniels stuttered out, not daring to look Winston in the eye. "Frederick..." he swallowed. "Frederick might have the skill to wield a sai."

Winston continued reviewing the reports and evidence, his mind far from eased, his heart heavy with the task at hand. The dockworker. The go-kart track. The sai. The confrontations over the go-kart. The timelines adding up just so... Suspicions were nothing until proven in the court of law. But still, it was a start. Time to pay Frederick a visit.

Clouds hovered above the go-kart track as Winston surveyed the murder scene. The sight of Gary's lifeless body had been replaced by yellow police tape, but the stain of what had occurred remained imprinted in Winston's mind.

Indisputably, Gary was the current go-kart champion of their small town. A title that endowed him a sense of invincibility and an obstacle for Jerome, the runner up more times than Jerome cared to admit.

Winston pulled the collar of his coat up, glancing around the track at the groups of people, all huddled up and whispering. Among the crowd, his eyes locked onto a man standing alone, pressing binoculars to his eyes. It was a quirk of Jerome's to carry binoculars, even to social gatherings. The man was Jerome, a local driving instructor.

As Winston approached, he saw numerous people trying to engage with Jerome. He seemed to be in his own world, unresponsive to those attempting to speak with him. His attention constantly straying elsewhere, ears tilted towards passing conversations as if eavesdropping. Winston couldn’t help but notice the insular behavior of the man.
"You're Jerome, right?" Winston asked. The man gave him a nod, his gaze fixed on the distant track. Jerome's listless eyes betrayed not apathy but a high passion for go-karting.

Jerome and Gary shared this passion, Winston learned, their go-kart rivalry was quite the spectacle in the local area. Contentious races, frequently ending with Gary taking the championship title very heatedly debated, and it was just a week ago when Gary accused Jerome of cheating.

"In his own world, isn't he?" commented one of the local racers, watching Winston's attempt to engage Jerome. "I've heard them arguing a lot recently. Especially after the last race..." he glanced at the silent Jerome.

Winston noted to visit the local gym, where Jerome had been seen practicing fight moves occasionally. The man was known to have a certificate of martial arts mastery as well. That singled him out, especially considering the nature of the murder weapon, a sai.

Thinking of sai, a cold wave of realization spread through him. He had seen a receipt in Jerome's office for multiple such weapons, and rumor had it that Jerome had been spotted purchasing multiple sais only a week back.

As the evening wind picked up, Winston took one last look at the solitary figure of Jerome. He was engrossed in his own world even in a crowded gathering. Suspicion, it would seem, wore many masks. It was time, Winston decided, to uncover the truth.

rounds.evidence_text: When Wendy's life brutally ended under the sharp end of a pickaxe at the local roller rink, it was up to the shrewd Detective Winston to untangle the web spun around two prime suspects, Marianne and Sidney.

Winston ran his fingers through his tangled hair as he fixated on the aged screen of the department’s underfunded monitor. It projected grainy CCTV footage of his suspect - Marianne. She was there at the roller rink, on the night poor Wendy met her end. Not only was Marianne there - she was seen shouting at Wendy, their voices escalating until they pierced the rhythmic hum of the skating wheels. The timestamp of the argument, and subsequent footage of Marianne lingering, suggested she was there for quite some time after her dispute with Wendy.

He thumbed through a thin folder tucked beneath a closing pizza box resting on his cluttered desk. Marianne had a criminal record, it revealed a past fraught with moments of explosion, of violence - including an assault arrest five years prior. The Marianne on the screen, the Marianne in these documents had been caught in the wrong before. Winston began to feel a creeping uneasiness as he parsed this correlation.

Several pictures tumbled from the folder as Winston shuffled its contents. The pictures were snapshots of Marianne: caught in the midst of her day-to-day, widely recognized by the community - not just for her nature but for her frequent use of an old pickaxe. It came as no surprise since she had spent several years working in the mines before her marriage. She was seen using her pickaxe for numerous tasks such as chopping firewood or loosening soil in her garden.

"Did you see what she was doing last week?" a seasoned woman down the road had mentioned as she was reversing her car out of the driveway. Marianne was seen cleaning her well-worn mining equipment that she'd kept stored in an easily accessible tool-shed next to her house in clear sight. It seemed she wasn't shy about flaunting her past or the tools she used while in the mines.

Commotion at the precinct broke Winston from his thoughts. The crime-scene analyst reported the murder took place in some remote corner of the roller rink. Despite the public dispute that took place earlier between Wendy and Marianne, this location seemed isolated, uncanny for such a busy locale.

The analyst's words seemed to chisel further into Winston's thoughts as he returned to the grainy images. Her mining equipment was never far from reach, and Marian's cacophony on the night of Wendy's murder was caught on tape.

Pieces started falling into place; too many strings tethered Marianne to the night Wendy was murdered. With a sigh, Winston allowed himself a quiet moment. Then, taking a deep breath, he began his descent into the intricacies of the case before him.

Winston stood at the entrance of the roller rink, eyes scanning the room. The images from the crime scene report replayed in his memory. Poor Wendy had breathed her last in what was supposed to be a place filled with the rejuvenating sounds of retro music and flashing lights.

Sidney, who was a geologist, had been seen with Wendy at the roller rink multiple times. According to the staff, Sidney was even a regular here. It was a curious detail but not unusual, people had hobbies apart from their professions. Sidney's passion besides analyzing layers of earth was rollerblading. He frequently carried his tools, including his pickaxe, from his daytime geological survey sites directly to the roller rink in the evenings.

Checking his notes from the previous conversation with Sidney, his eyebrows knitted slightly as he remembered the desperation he sensed from Sidney. It revolved around Wendy, who apparently knew something he coveted as a secret. She had been sharing this secret with her friends and it seemed it held the power to publicly humiliate Sidney if it ever came to light. Sidney, for his part, vehemently denied any secret of such scale.

Winston gestured for the barista to come over. The young man with a skater haircut glanced at Winston's badge before he ordered a black coffee with no sugar. While waiting for his order, he asked, “Did you notice Sidney here during the time of the incident?”
The barista nodded, nervously biting his lower lip. "Yes, Detective. Sidney was here. I remember seeing him."

Winston nodded as he continued his observations. His gaze lingered over Sidney's station where he parked his geologist’s gear, including his trusted pickaxe, which he used during his geological field trips, when he visited. He noticed the stains of usual wear and tear and a freshly cleaned pickaxe leaning against the wall. Nothing unusual for a geologist. Taking down notes, Winston silently queued the information; the same Pickaxe might have been used for the murder.

His phone buzzed breaking his trail of thoughts, He took the informer's call. He glanced at his watch noting down the time of the conversation before disconnecting the call. He finished his coffee and left the roller rink. He had to confirm if Wendy was indeed telling the truth about that secret or Sidney was just an innocent geologist who loved rollerblading and hated gossips.

rounds.evidence_text: In the hushed sanctity of a bustling synagogue, Vanessa's life was abruptly ended with a common tool, and now Detective Winston must unravel the tangled threads of suspicion around Ivy and Clarence.

As Detective Winston carefully leafed through the day’s case files, an unusual detail caught his eye. The murder that occurred in a local synagogue, and the victim's name, Vanessa, stirred up an old memory. After what he had seen, quitting had often filled his thoughts. But solving cases like these held an irreplaceable allure to Winston’s trouble-stricken mind.

His first lead came in the form of an irregular character by the name Clarence. A truck driver who works long hours, regularly present near the synagogue amongst other stops, and oddly enough, an ardent collector of obituaries. Often, community members would speak in hushed tones of Clarence’s nightly tears shed over obituaries, forming an image of emotional investment over people he had no known connection with. Despite their gossiping, none of them had ever heard of Clarence befriending or nurturing a relationship with anyone mentioned in the obituaries. In fact, during their investigation, the police found no documented ties of Clara with the deceased individuals, either.

Over black coffee and stale bread in a nearby diner, Detective Winston conversed with Clarence. "So you’re a truck driver? Tough gig, I imagine," Winston started the conversation the way he always did, meandering towards his point while observing reactions.

"You bet. I've been doing this job for a while now, driving all sorts of routes. Comes with its own set of challenges, like finding a decent mechanic on the go. I had to learn repairing my truck on my own. Hence, the toolbox you see me lugging around," Clarence responded.
Detective Winston veered the discussion towards Vanessa, "And what brings you around the synagogue frequently?"

"Well, work mostly. But it’s no secret - Vanessa, she and me... We used to be together. She'd often be at the synagogue. Despite how things ended with us, my old habits never really changed," Clarence replied with a forlorn sigh.

As Winston remembered Vanessa's face and Clarence's haggard expression, sleep felt like a distant luxury. Skimming through the raw facts in his notebook, this was no game of conjectures, the hard evidence was yet to fit in the puzzle. And with that last thought, he closed the notebook shut for the night.

Detective Winston stood, perched in the corner of the local hardware store. He watched from behind a pyramid of paint cans, peering at Ivy as she demonstrated a new set of screwdrivers to a customer. Overalls clad, she seemed like an everyday, hard-working woman. She completed the sale and moved on to help the next customer, carrying another set of similar tools to the customer who was looking for a specific size. It was clear that she moved deftly and knew her products well.

It troubled Winston how an ordinary day selling hardware could be turned on its head so rapidly, by a single piece of information. Winston decided to make his move. He stepped out from his hiding place, adjusting the collar of his trench coat to protect from the sudden gust of wind that swept through the open door.
“Hello, Ivy,” he said, his gaze piercing through her.

Dropping her head down, the terror and desperation in Ivy’s eyes were evident. Caught in a blackmail situation over deep secrets that Vanessa had threatened to reveal, secrets that could ruin her reputation, it was serving harsh punishments on her livelihood in the form of lost customers. She feared her secrets would come out any day now. It was this fear that had greeted Winston when Ivy arrived at the synagogue that morning, noticeably before Vanessa's life was tragically ended there.

Refusing to meet his gaze, she nodded, inviting him to continue.   "We belong to the same community," Winston said nonchalantly. "How about those services at the synagogue? You usually attend weekly, right? Speaking of, I couldn't help but notice you were the first to arrive on the fateful morning Vanessa was killed."
“Ye-yes,” Ivy stuttered, caught off guard.
"Wonderful sermons," Winston went on, "I heard about the incident at the synagogue, terrible loss for us all. Vanessa was such a wonderful woman."
A tightening grip around her own worn hands was the only sign from Ivy that she felt the weight and severity of the situation, she offered a low, mournful "Yes," in agreement.
The gloom was creeping in, matching the evident fear, and Winston fiddled with the notepad in his hands. He had one more stop to make before he was done for the day.

"I'll be seeing you around, Ivy," he left her to tend to her work still reeling from the effects of the ongoing blackmail. It was a bit troubling news for a woman who seemed to be losing her livelihood amidst the desperation and fear that she was immersed in.

Winston left the store, the falling sun casting long shadows. Ivy’s secrets were her own, whatever they were. It was something he knew Vanessa had threatened to reveal, which now loom over her existence. There was a chill in the air, much like the uncertainty that hung over the case.

Ivy stood there, amidst rows and shelves of tools and hardware equipment she sold daily, in a store that had been affected by the blackmail. Despite demonstrating tools like screwdrivers all day, every day, she was no murderer, and Winston knew that the truth would ultimately reveal itself.

rounds.evidence_text: When Mack's life got fatally bleached out on a soccer field, it was up to Detective Winston to sift through the dark clues left by his suspects: Helen and Danielle.

Winston, his heart heavy with grim resolution, studied the photos of Mack's lifeless body on the soccer field. The murder scene was an unsavory juxtaposition of innocence - usually bustling with kids, laughter, and vibrant life, now tainted with the solemnity of demise and the faint smell of bleach lingering in the air.
His next step was Helen, Mack's sole testamentary beneficiary it seemed, and his housekeeper - a critical point of interest.

Arriving at the soccer field, he spotted Helen from afar, scrubbing away at the stubborn grass stains with a generous amount of bleach - a daily routine in her housekeeping duties. She was an efficient worker, with knowledge on various cleaning products and supplies, which her job demanded.
His eyes became glued to a large quantity of bleach that Helen had with her. An unsettling thought crossed his mind, quickly followed by a dismissive wave.

Winston introduced himself to Helen who was already there. Judging by her demeanor, he got an underlying sense of humiliation boiling within her, perhaps a result of being objectified at her job as a housekeeper.
"Do you clean up after the games every time?" Winston asked, breaking the tense silence.
"Every single time. They don't clean up after themselves, so someone's got to do it," Helen said, her tone full of regrettable resignation, showing no signs of withholding information.
"So, you were here, even when the game was on?" Winston then asked, the seemingly benign query holding a latent inquiry.
“Yes, and Mr. Mack, bless his soul, stayed behind with me after everyone else had left,” Helen replied, burrowing her frown even further, eyes welling up with unseen tears.
She continued talking away, inadvertently revealing how she's often at the rough end of some nasty backbiting, making Winston wonder if that might've fuelled her self-diminution.
"Are you Mack's housekeeper?" Winston asked, out of the blue, seemingly testing Helen's patience.

She stared at him for a solid minute before affirming she was, indeed, Mack's housekeeper. Mack, she recalled, even included Helen's role in his will, stating that she should run the house in the event of his untimely demise.
With an interview like this, it was hard not to observe how it all seemed to add up, but Winston prudently kept his findings to himself.

As Winston returned to his car, he remembered Mack, a man with no family, found dead right after one such soccer game Helen was apparently cleaning up for. He also remembered an incident involving Helen from the past – an unfortunate mishap where a staff member had accidentally ingested a cleaning supply.
"Interesting," Winston muttered to himself, starting his car. "Very interesting indeed."
This was going to be a long case.

Winston idly flicked through the passport he had received from a fellow officer, who found it thrown aside at the soccer field, where teenagers often conjugated. "Maria," he read aloud from the passport photo. He flipped it over to find another stamp from Denmark and a passport photo stapled to the back – "Chloe, Denmark." Holy hell, what a lead.

Turning his attention to the crime scene, it wasn't long before Detective Winston found himself on the doorstep of Danielle, the local spiritual guru, alternatively known as Maria and Chloe in her past.

Danielle's reputation preceded her not just for her aliases but also for her meticulous cleaning which she considered a spiritual activity. "It's a form of meditation for me, I find serenity in cleanliness," Danielle replied to Winston's gentle ribbing, with a slight smile.
"Is that why you’re against Mack's wedding?" Winston asked. She blinked at him. "Rumor has it, you've taken quite the interest in Mack's so called love-life."

Danielle, in her belief of spiritual purity, confessed, "Harmful karmic consequences often ensue when one person pledges themselves to someone they do not love. Mack was about to please his parents by making such a mistake, marrying a woman he didn't care for. I wanted Mack to remain single, as I believe it would have maintained his spiritual purity."

She paused to siphon some tea from a kettle, her eyes never leaving Winston. "By the way, Detective, I think you’ve dropped something," she said, pointing at the passport Winston had forgotten in his jacket pocket. "Oh, that?" he asked nonchalantly, "It's your passport, isn’t it? Maria, Chloe, all your aliases, found at the crime scene."

Danielle gave it a fleeting glance and said, "Ah I see, Detective. Still, it's not the one I use currently... I don't need a passport to travel. I have lived in many places under many names, including Sophie in France."
Winston kicked a stone down the road as he left Danielle's residence, pondering on her confessions. "Sophie, France", he mumbled to himself. More identities. More questions.

Back at the station, he poured over the evidence once more which also had multiples items linking Danielle to the alias Sophie in France. Mack was about to wed a woman he didn’t love just to please his parents... and there he lay on the soccer field, with the smell of bleach fresh in his throat. The same bleach that Mack’s spiritual guru, Maria, Chloe, Sophie, Danielle would stock in volumes almost crazy enough to put a cleaning supply store out of business.
What a case.

rounds.evidence_text: In the chilling silence of a serene campground, Ernest meets his untimely end by a crowbar; now, it's up to the keen instincts of Detective Winston to unravel the mystery with only two suspects: Addison and Octavia.

Winston scratched his head as he reviewed the case files, his gaze lingering on the photo of the victim, Ernest. The sight of the young boy stretched out lifeless in the woodland was an image too jarring to easily forget.

Dropping his files onto the table, Winston decided to visit the scene of the crime, the local campground where Ernest and many others had gathered for a large party. As Winston walked around the now abandoned campsite, he noticed a few items left behind by the careless partygoers. It was here Ernest had been found, brutally murdered with a crowbar.
Addison, a classmate of Ernest and a regular at the campsite, had been present on the day of the murder. Winston had his eye on him, based on the information he'd received.

Next, Winston decided to pay Addison a visit at his place of work. As an apprentice mechanic, Addison spent his days working hard in the garage, using a variety of tools. The garage was a mess of wrenches, screwdrivers, and yes, even a few crowbars. It seemed only natural for a mechanic to possess such tools.
“Detective Winston. To what do I owe this pleasure?” Addison greeted him as he entered the garage, leisurely cleaning his hands with a rag.
Winston showed his badge, “ Investigating the murder of Ernest.”
“Yeah, very sad stuff,” Addison said sighing heavily. "Ernie and I went way back. Even went camping together at the same site."

Digging further into Addison's background, Winston found that this small-town mechanic apprentice was surprisingly also a scholar. He had been accepted, on scholarship, to a prestigious college based on his impressive grades.

Impressive, unless you got wind that perhaps not all of his grades were honestly won. Winston found out that Addison indeed did cheat on a major exam. This was not unusual, save that Ernest knew about it and had threatened to go public, potentially jeopardizing the prestigious scholarship.

As Winston confined his investigation for the day, he couldn't help but remember what Addison had said, "Getting that scholarship, it's my ticket out of this town," he had said. Then he’d paused, rubbing the back of his neck before adding sheepishly, "It could be revoked though, if my grades were to suddenly drop."
And so the day came to a close, and Winston was left with his thoughts. But something told him that this case was far from being resolved.

Detective Winston rolled up to the police station for the task laid before him. Busy with daily hustle and tasks, it wasn't an unfamiliar sight, but today it felt unusual. He was at the station to interview one of the very ones who uphold the law – Octavia.

Approaching her desk, he saw Octavia fiddling around with her phone before tucking it away hastily. Winston noticed her coworker attentively watching Octavia, before briefly meeting his eyes and offering a sheepish nod. "I saw her deleting some of those social media apps off her phone this morning," the coworker whispered as Winston passed by him. He added quickly, "I could recognize the logos before she removed them."
Taking a seat by Octavia, Winston introduced himself, while subtly inspecting Octavia. She seemed alert and in control - typical traits of a trained officer.
After a brief conversation about her duties, Winston asked, "I hear you were on patrol last night?"
"Yeah, I was," Octavia responded with a steady voice, maintaining eye contact with Winston.
"Did your route include the campgrounds?” Winston queried but Octavia was already nodding, her face passive.

Winston, attempting to glean more from her body language, asked for a photograph of her for reference. "I am afraid that's not possible," she responded tersely. "I don’t allow photographs of me to be taken. Privacy is valuable to me."
With this, she offered a polite smile, excusing herself to attend to her duties. Winston nodded, got up, and left the station.

Later on, he found himself at the campgrounds where Ernest was killed. The site was filled with chatter and murmurs of curiosity. Many among the crowd knew of Ernest who had somewhat of a reputation for exposing secrets.

Winston learned that Ernest had discovered Octavia's secret illegal activities carried out long back in her past. Moreover, he discovered a draft email on Ernest's phone, intended to be an expose of Octavia, indicating that Ernest was planning to reveal this secret. A secret – now known to him and evidently, Ernest himself – which Octavia would have wanted desperately, especially to kept hidden from her colleagues, from the department itself.
At a party, she was heard saying, "I value my privacy more than anything." This reassured Winston of her dedication to keeping her past hidden.
As dusk set on the campgrounds, Winston recollected the events of the day pondering his next move.

rounds.evidence_text: When Letti's lifeless body is found horrifically mutilated by a machete at a secluded mountain cabin, gritty Detective Winston faces a chilling whodunit featuring suspects Delilah and Eddie.

Gazing out at the tranquil scenery of the mountain cabin where Letti met her end, detective Winston pondered the information before him. He had another interview to conduct, and as the mountain breeze tousled his rigid hair, he couldn't help but be reminded of this case's unnerving details.

Eddie was an interesting character, to say the least. A musician of sorts, he was known for incorporating tricks using a machete into his performances. A peculiar stage craft that Winston couldn't begin to comprehend. Performing such stunts would require him to practice, possibly during his free time he spent camping on the outskirts of the city, with his trusted machete always by his side.

The mountain cabin reverberated with somber silence as Winston approached Eddie. He had been staying at the same cabin, having been invited by Letti for a song recording. It was reported that during his stay that Eddie had no other engagements to attend to; an oddity given that this time of year was bustling with music festivals.
"How's the stay been, Eddie?" Winston began, trying to ease Eddie into the conversation.
"Quiet," Eddie responded, his gaze drifting off into the vast span of the desolate mountainscape. "Just how I like it, you know. Helps with the creativity."

There was an aromatic air to Eddie, of someone who had worked tirelessly to uphold their image in the light of public scrutiny. It was well-known that Eddie was sensitive about his image, keen to maintain the rising trajectory of his music career, a career he held close to his heart.

The cabin’s solitude was a stark reminder of what was at stake for Eddie. Letti, the soulful songbird she was, had managed to unravel a hidden part of Eddie's life that threatened to shatter the glass tower he had been building over the years: his secret drug addiction. Unfortunately, the discovery gave Letti the leverage to manipulate Eddie's successful music career.
Winston kept an attentive poker face while internally connecting the pieces of information.
"The thing is, Eddie," Winston began, his tone sober, "Letti wouldn't have invited you over for any ordinary recording."
"I know," Eddie sighed heavily before he added, "She held my career in her hands, detective."

His confession resounded through the empty cabin, the once picturesque view from the window shading into a grim canvas of their situation. With no one around for miles, Winston wondered what influence this isolation could have on the psyche of the person who was here.
"I reckon we meet again, detective," Eddie said, his voice just above a whisper, as Winston left the cabin.

Detective Winston pulled his car up to the secluded cabin. His visit was to Delilah, the godmother of the recently slain Letti. So far, the only evidence he had found was a machete, smeared with blood.

He knocked on the heavy oak door of her abode and Delilah greeted him with a passive stare. Before he could utter a word, she gestured him inside and they both sat down to chat. Delilah, interestingly, made it a point to hang her machete over the fireplace, “Papa taught me to handle a machete since I was teen. I live out here alone in the wilderness, y'know, just as precaution.” she justified.

Their conversation flowed smoothly until Winston asked Delilah about her past. Instantly, the woman fell silent, her gaze fixed on a spot on the wall, as if she was lost in thought. She curtly responded, "I had a normal, happy childhood. That's all." Winston was struck by this as he knew from others' accounts that no one had ever heard her talk about her childhood or school days in detail.

Winston decided not to probe further, giving Delilah space to guide the conversation. This led her to casually mention her skills with a machete. Come to think of it, she’d won several local machete handling competitions. "I practice regularly," she added, a briefly proud glint in her eyes.

Winston nodded in acknowledgment, his mind returning to documents found in Letti’s possession. These documents seemed to implicate Delilah in some illegal activities. Letti reiteratively voiced concern about her godmother's activities. In fact, she had directly confronted Delilah about the evidence she’d stumbled upon. Even more alarmingly, Letti had confided in her friends about her intention to go public with this evidence.

Letti’s friends shared with Winston how she was deeply worried about Delilah's suspicious activities; however, the specific details of her past remained obscured. Winston took a last glance at the machete hanging over the fireplace before leaving the cabin, a sense of unsettling curiosity lingering in his mind.

rounds.evidence_text: In the shimmering opulence of a luxury restaurant, Roderick's life was abruptly ended by a pistol's merciless blow; now Detective Winston must untangle the web of Oscar and Brianna's testimonies.

Detective Winston sat down in the interview room with a sigh, glancing at the woman before him. Brianna, a teacher by profession. Her face etched with confusion and a hint of defiance painted an intriguing story.
"So, Brianna, let me understand this," Winston began. "You work at the local school, is that correct?"
"That's right," Brianna said, a look of challenge in her eyes.
"And during a recent meeting, you were discussing matters about your class?" Winston asked.
"I was giving an update on student performance," Brianna responded, her voice strong and assertive.

Just then, a school official, the school's principal, entered the interview room unexpectedly. A look of concern was etched on his face. "May I have a moment with my staff members, Detective?" he asked, pleading with his eyes.

Winston sighed and nodded, exiting the room. He knew from the principal that not only was Brianna not given the promotion she was considered for, but the decision had come from her colleague Roderick – he had outright refused to consider her for promotion. Feeling slighted, she had a heated argument with Roderick at school.

Winston knew, Brianna was capable. She had won several shooting competitions but her recent activity showed a disturbing pattern. His colleague had told him earlier that Brianna was seen practicing with a pistol at the shooting range. A pistol that matched the murder weapon used.

Further investigation led him to a public event. Brianna was present with companions, putting on a friendly face and a casual mask of normalcy. A perfect alibi. But Winston wasn't entirely convinced just yet.
He recalled a field policeman questioning Brianna about her job as a teacher. A brave woman confident in her role, but her world had been recently rocked by disappointment.
A rival teacher had been promoted instead of her. And Brianna, a competitive woman herself, seemed to be harboring some hard feelings.

Winston made his way back to the interrogation room. Brianna, his current person of interest, had recently purchased the same kind of pistol used in Roderick's murder. That fact alone made him cautiously alert.

This case was far from over, leaving Winston to piece together the complex web of evidence and suspect motives. He sighed, looking across the table at the woman in front of him, contemplating the next steps in his investigation.

Detective Winston sighed as he ran his fingers through his hair looking over the crime scene photographs. The sight of Roderick, a successful entrepreneur, found at a luxury restaurant, oddly felt disheartening to Winston.

From his collected evidence, a pistol registered to Oscar's name was used to shoot Roderick. Winston thought back to the office reports he'd reviewed: Oscar recently losing his job and multiple reports of conflicts at the office. This was a man grappling with a world that was unraveling.

As he drove to Oscar's residence for an interview, Winston couldn't shake the image of the domestic dispute reports mentioned by Oscar's children. They fell into a pattern with Oscar's recent purchase of a gun and his prescribed therapy for divorce-related depression.

Detective Winston studied the forums online, seeking information about tour destinations in the rural farmland area where Mackenzie had met his end during a guided tour. He stumbled upon a chalet managed by a woman named Yolanda.

As Winston hit the road, his thoughts steered towards the information he had gathered. Mackenzie had been part of Yolanda's tour group before his murder occurred on the eve of their scheduled contact. She managed her tours in the countryside meticulously. The control she had over the schedule of the outings, including the fateful one in which Mackenzie was murdered, intrigued Winston.

His mind drifted back to the victim. Mackenzie had found out about Yolanda's past, a string of cheating instances involving her tour clients, and the woman bore a lengthy criminal record as a result. In fact, Mackenzie was under the impression that she had conned him out of money as well, and he had evidence to prove so. Hence, the threats of exposure he made just before the tour, threatening to bring down Yolanda's whole charade if she didn't pay him off.

Winston yanked the steering wheel to his jeep, steering it down a rural path as he followed the coordinates to the chalet. The area was primarily farmland, a quiet countryside where the chalet sat nestled. Yolanda worked here, a guide amidst the rustic charm and tranquility, where such unfortunate events as Mackenzie's murder took place.

Approaching the chalet, Winston observed the tools strewn around the land nearby, tools that weren't entirely uncommon to such rural regions. That included the sickle, commonly used for tough manual jobs done by locals during tours.

"Detective, may I help you?" A woman called, her hands resting on her hips as she presented a robust picture of strength and resilience. Her firm tone and her hardened features attested to her familiarity with tough manual labor. Yolanda was her name, the tour guide of the chalet where Mackenzie was last seen alive during her tour.
"Yes, Yolanda, right?" Winston treaded carefully, pacing his sentences.
"That's correct, detective," She replied, her gaze steady, "This chalet, it's a part of the tour destinations I manage."
"You work around these areas quite a bit then?" Winston probed, his eyes scanning the area.
"That's right," Yolanda said, her hands sweeping the landscape, "My tours consist of these rural areas, I find the countryside soothing."
"So I heard," Winston nodded, tucking away a piece of information about the murder happening during one of these tours, as he turned to retreat.

Winston was a man of the city, yet he found himself drawn to the tranquility of the chalet nestled in the snowy mountains. This tranquility was disrupted by the gruesome murder of the chalet's owner, Mackenzie. No heirs, all that was left was a cold case just like the winter’s harsh weather.

His main puzzle piece at the moment was Julius. As far as Winston had gathered, Julius was frequently seen around the chalet courting religious duties. A Rabbi with admiration for Mackenzie's business, he pondered as he moved through the chalet.

Brushing off the snow from his overcoat, he walked down to Julius's residence. He found his neighbour out, tending to his plants, who readily shared with Winston his observations about the Rabbi. “Late nights, buddy, that's when you hear it! Car cleaning noises. Almost ritualistic, you might say.” He gestured with a chuckle towards Julius's car that appeared glistening clean even in the morning frost.

Keeping his poker face intact, Winston thanked him and moved on to Julius's place to gain some firsthand perspective. Julius, next of kin, was willing to engage with Winston. "I was at the chalet both times,” he conceded, “In the morning to pay my respects, in the evening for my religious duties. I express no remorse for my actions.”

Seeing the need to switch the conversation to less stringent matters, Winston asked about Julius's frequent trips to the auto-parts store. The rabbi, a bit taken aback, chuckled and affirmed, “Ah, you mean the cleaning supplies? Yes, I don't like to keep my car dirty. A friend of mine, a car enthusiast, once saw me buying in bulk and joked I was preparing for apocalypse.”

Julius voiced no regret for his admiration towards Mackenzie's business. His eyes filled with fond memories, he added, “Our community often frowned upon his lack of religious beliefs, but I admired him. His open-mindedness is to be celebrated. Even in mourning I believe it’s important to remember the good.”

Winston returned to the cold chalet. Julius was indeed a complex character, but he was on a mission to uncover the truth. What did Julius do the night of the murder? With Mackenzie’s time of death set in the evening, he wondered what the events were that unfolded in this chalet. The detective in him would not rest until all the pieces of the puzzle come together. Murders, after all, can happen where you least expect them to.

rounds.evidence_text: In the chilling underbelly of a secluded bunker, Donald's life was snuffed out by deadly snake venom and now, it's up to the sharp and relentless Detective Winston to shake the truth out of his prime suspects, Jay and Autumn.

Winston squinted in the dim bunker light, glancing around at the empty shelves and overturned furniture; the area decked with caution tapes. Something didn't sit right, there was always more to the story than what laid bare, Winston knew this.

His latest lead led him to Autumn, the only person Donald would have willingly let inside his survival bunker. Before Donald’s unanticipated retreat to his bunker, he had mentioned his intent to her. The two of them were old acquaintances, sharing a history few knew of, having been in a criminal gang together. Donald was more trusting than most, in fact, Autumn was the only person he would trust when it came to sharing such a secluded spot. His survival bunker was his safe haven, where he was known to retreat when the world became too loud.

Maybe it was her psychic abilities that drew him in - Autumn did have a knack for knowing things before they happened. Or maybe it was her unique collection of pets she so lovingly tended to. Her pets came with a singular bite, a serpentine collection that few dared to keep. As the sole caretaker of these reptiles, she also had intimate knowledge of their venom, which she knew could prove deadly for Donald.

Even fewer knew about Autumn's illicit past, dark secrets tangled up with crimes committed years ago; secrets that could have turned disastrous had they been revealed. She feared the consequences that awaited her, fearing her darkest secrets could be unveiled leading to her undoing.
And then there was Donald. He had always been a reliable man. A straight shooter who stood up for what he believed was right, even if it got in the way of his personal well-being.
"I'd heard a rumor, Autumn," started Winston, meeting her outside her reptile enclosure, "Heard that Donald found out you were back to your old tricks."
Autumn's eyes widened just a tiny bit, almost imperceptible, a reaction only someone with Winston's training would catch.
"Imagine his surprise," continued Winston, "down in the bunker alone, knowing his old friend is involved in illegal matters again."
Autumn was silent, staring at the detective with an unreadable expression.

Donald's fatal allergy to snake venom was not a widely known fact, but one that Autumn was well aware of. Yet, Winston couldn't help but notice, but Autumn's snakes seemed to be unfazed and peaceful in their glass enclosures. Unusual for creatures known for their deadly bite.
It struck Winston odd as he mindfully stepped away from the enclosure, keeping Autumn under gaze, "I hope you aren't up to no good, Autumn, because secrets always find their way out."

Winston took another sip of his lukewarm coffee as he glanced upon the crime scene photos spread out on his desk. Donald's murder was an unusual one, a death by snake venom. He had always thought that underground bunkers were safe; this case was proving him wrong.

Word on the street was that Jay was quite the character. A missionary, stationed in a region notorious for snakes, missionaries of that region were trained to extract snake venom due to the frequent encounters with these creatures. Winston lit a cigarette as he thought about Jay's training. It seemed unusual for a man of god, but Winston quickly reminded himself that his job was not to question, rather to understand.
He stepped out of his office, coffee in hand, and made his way to the local church. He had arranged to meet Jay there, hoping to gather some insights to this peculiar case.

Jay was adjusting the chairs in the church when Winston walked in. As he approached Jay helping his surroundings, Winston couldn't help but notice the lack of both vocal inflection and changing facial expressions in Jay's greetings. Adding to that, Jay never gave away a hint of his personal life during their meeting, always twisting the conversation towards his missionary tales.

Despite this, Winston listened attentively. Jay's stories were filled with accounts of handling snakes, a talent he came to master during his time in the region. But as the detective prodded for more personal information, Jay grew restless and god forbid, began to show signs of emotion, expertly redirecting the conversation to a less personal level.

Home from his meeting with Jay, Winston could not ignore the oddities. Jay was engaging but avoided personal questions. He was in a place full of snakes and had experience handling them. But could handling snakes lead to killing someone?

A conversation with a certain Father McNulty led to a shocking revelation. Jay was allegedly smuggling drugs during his mission trips. It was a serious accusation, but if true, it could certainly pile on disastrous professional and personal consequences.

Snakebites remedies were common knowledge among missionaries, it became clear. A darker thought hit Winston, Jay had both access and expertise in handling snake venom--a fact that couldn't be overlooked.

The final piece to the puzzle came from James, a local grocery-hand who had heard Donald confront Jay about the drugs. It hadn't gone too well. Consequently, this planted a seed of doubt in Winston's mind.

Jay had managed to combine what seemed like an altruistic role of a missionary with illicit activities. But the question remained--did he escalate these actions to murder? Winston stubbed out his cigarette and let out a tired puff of smoke. It would be a long night sorting through his clues.

rounds.evidence_text: In the shimmering depths of a popular scuba diving site, Julian's life was brutally extinguished with a crowbar; now, it's up to Detective Winston to dive into the murky secrets of suspects Lucy and Clara.

While examining the photos from the murder scene, Detective Winston couldn't help but feel a chill crawl up his spine. Beneath the bubbles, the crime scene lay at the bottom of the ocean, a place that was supposed to be a sanctuary for divers like Julian.

His train of thought was interrupted by his partner who handed him a pile of interview transcripts and surveillance files to go through. He was about to dive into the world of their main suspect, Clara.

Coming from a workstation that was perpetually cluttered with stacks of serial killer novels, Clara no doubt had a keen interest in the subject matter. She was frequently engrossed in conversations about infamous serial killers, delving into their modus operandi with unsettling accuracy without any need for references. During her lunch breaks, she could always be found pouring over one of her many true crime books.

Clara, a skilled metal worker, had a specific niche in crafting a variety of unique crowbars, which had become her signature work. Her craftsmanship was distinct and always earned her respect amongst her peers. Going through a surveillance tape, he watched as Clara loaded her uniquely crafted crowbar into her vehicle before heading out to the diving site. The crowbar didn't seem out of place, what with her being a metal worker and competitively acknowledged for her unique metalwork.

Her performance at work had been nothing short of outstanding, and she had been putting in long, overtime hours. She was highly dedicated to her work and never missed an opportunity to express her ambition for a promotion.

Julian and Clara both worked at the same company, and both had been in the running for the same promotion. During the office water cooler chats, he'd heard Clara express her keen interest in the promotion, and her evident disappointment when Julian became a potential contender.

The evidence was laid in front of him: a woman with an enthusiastic interest in killers, always reading her crime books even on her lunch breaks, a craftsman with a signature touch on uniquely crafted crowbars, and seen with one on the day of Julian's infamous dive. A metal worker who had been putting in long hours for an impressive performance. All that tied with the delicate balance of coworkers both competing for the same promotion.

One piece of evidence caught his eye. Clara was also a part of the diving team on the day Julian was murdered. With that, Winston pushed back his chair, stood up, and prepared to pay Clara a visit. He had a feeling there would be more to dig up from her perpetually stacked workspace, files and statements during her interrogation.

Winston stood overlooking the gentle sway of the ocean, the sun reflecting a glaring path of light towards the spot where Julian's body had been found. The dive was a secluded affair, intended just for a small, close-knit group of divers which included Lucy and Julian, often dive partners.

Derailing his thoughts, he flicked through his notes, focusing on Lucy's background - the woman had a varied history, from construction sites to docks, her hand attending to many trades. She'd even taken a boat maintenance course somewhere along the way. A crowbar tool was commonly used in both professions.
"Detective Winston, Miss Lucy is ready to see you," a uniformed officer approached him.
"Thank you, officer," he responded, shaking his head in dismissal, his eyes still on the open files in his hand.
He walked into the impromptu interview room, eyes finding Lucy easily. She looked out of place in the cold, steel-colored room, her complexion still holding on to the sun-kissed hue from the sail.
"Lucy," Winston began, his tone neutral. "You and Julian. I've been told you two dive together frequently," he watched her face for any signs of reaction.
"Yes," she confirmed curtly. "Julian and I...we were friends," she added before a tight swallow. "He betrayed my trust though, caused me significant trouble."
That drew his attention. He decided to delve into the more intimate details, "You were managing the tools for this trip?"
Caught off guard, Lucy straightened. "Yes...yes, that's correct. I've always taken care of the gear, packed the crowbar too. Just a precaution..."
"I see. Just a precaution," he repeated.
Catching her eye, he questioned further, "Lucy, did you overhear Julian discussing this betrayal?"
A flicker of shock passed over her face. "Yes...with someone I didn't recognize," she admitted.
Another clue. He asked, "Lucy, did you find any evidence in Julian's belongings?"
"I... I found some documents in his gear locker...which I always thought only I could access," she confessed.
"Interesting. Very interesting," he nodded before standing up, preparing to leave but not before confirming one last detail.
"You shared the same boat, is that correct?"
"Yes," Lucy admitted, looking rather bewildered by the question.
"Very well," said Winston, concluding his interview and leaving Lucy to her thoughts, his mind buzzing with the new information and the unfolding mystery.

rounds.evidence_text: In the sweltering heat of the desert, Detective Winston finds himself amid the ashes of the flamethrower murder of Renee, with Paige and Marianne emerging as the prime suspects.

With a sigh of empathy, Detective Winston glanced over at a picture of Renee, the victim in his current case. Renee, the mentor of his current subject of interest in this case named Paige, was loved by many. She had always guided those under her with kindness but it seems even kindness isn’t enough to buy one safety.

Finding more peace in solitude, he decided to pay a visit to the same desert where Renee's charred remains were found. Even conveniently situated close to Paige's workshop, it didn't take long for him to drive there. Intriguingly enough, this visit happened on the same day, when a flamethrower was reported to have been delivered to Paige's workshop, according to the delivery company’s records.

His meetings with Paige always yielded new, interesting details. He noticed the transition of Paige's hair from short during their first encounter, to being long in the recent one. Along with that, he also took note of another change in her appearance on Monday - the color of her contacts. She was seen wearing blue contacts, unlike the green ones she was wearing during the Wednesday meeting.

Paige was a special effects expert, especially adept at managing flamethrowers, probably a reason for the flamethrower request at her special effects workshop. Something Paige had mentioned stood out to him, her desire to demonstrate something in the desert to Renee, her mentor.

Upon returning from the desert to Paige's workshop, the tech area was filled with different props and gadgets, all related to special effects. Among all, the flamethrower that she had requested stood out, it was identical to the one she was spotted with a few days back.
Tired and deep in thought, he took some quiet time to contemplate his findings, particularly about the chilling fact - Paige was the last person to be seen with Renee before she went missing.

As always, Winston's face remained mask-like, revealing nothing as he continued to probe and understand, focusing solely on gathering the facts of the chaotic mosaic before him. He knew there were many pieces yet to be put into place before the picture could begin to make sense.

Winston gazed over the desert horizon, letting his eyes rest on what felt like an infinite sea of sand. It was here where Renee's body was found, thoroughly torched, origins of which was thought to be a flamethrower.
He headed away from the scene, his mind whirling with questions and concerns, to conduct his next interview. His destination was a well-known cafe at the edge of town.

Marianne, the barista, had a strange calmness about her, despite being awaiting her punishment next week after being found guilty of theft. She didn’t flinch when she saw officer Winston approach - instead, she graciously offered him a cup of Joe. Around her, there was no evidence of anyone else's presence.
“Hello Marianne,” Winston made idle chat, “It must get pretty hot back here in the summers.”
“Surely does, but we’ve got it under control,” Marianne replied, sipping her coffee, “We've all done a thorough fire safety course.”
Winston nodded and decided to change the subject. “I heard you've recently visited the pawn shop and there seems to be a flamethrower missing after your visit”
“Sometimes, yeah, I shop there. Good old stuff comes cheap,” Marianne replied casually, not giving away any signs of panic.
“Any recent purchases?” Winston asked carefully.
“Can't recall,” Marianne quickly replied, her tone betraying nothing.
Winston shifted gears again, “Sounds like you have some travel plans? A solo road trip...”
Marianne shrugged, “I keep hearing about this desert route, figured I might give it a shot.”
“I hope you’ll travel safely. Deserts can be dangerous, y’know,” Winston remarked. "We found a woman's body there terribly torched..."
Before he could finish, Marianne held up a hand, “Renee, wasn’t it? She testified against me in court if you weren’t aware. Sad news for sure.”
“Indeed,” Winston nodded solemnly, “Indeed it is.” He finished his coffee and stood up to leave. “Good luck with your punishment next week, Marianne. See you around.”
With that, Winston left the coffee shop, ending the first round of this seemingly endless cycle of questions.

rounds.evidence_text: In the hushed silence of the library, Floyd lay dead with a shiv protruding from his chest, prompting Detective Winston to weave through the labyrinth of books and suspicion, targeting his primary suspects, Zara and Catherine.

Winston glanced over the crime scene again, the quiet library now a place of death and horror. The victim, Floyd, lay lifeless on the floor, an unlikely end to his ruthless pursuit of money. Floyd had refused to give up on collecting from Catherine, an airline pilot who had fallen on some hard times with missed mortgage payment after missed mortgage payment.

Stepping away from the crime scene, Winston called in a visit to Catherine. Her house felt quiet, almost sparse, a faint memory of better times perhaps reflected in something he noticed frequently in the past few weeks - her obsessively reading through her scrapbook, scanning, examining, dwelling in her past. It was hard to imagine a woman like Catherine having to sell her own plane, but interestingly enough, substantial debt and strain could cause people to do things they wouldn't ordinarily consider.

As Winston noticed Catherine walking up to the front door, an odd sight caught his eye. Catherine was holding her well-thumbed scrapbook in one hand, and newspaper clippings and obituaries littered the ground around her. A more careful look revealed an extensive collection of obituaries forming a large part of her scrapbook. The other hand held a familiar object – a pair of scissors – as she cut out pieces of articles to add to her collection. And discarded scrap clippings ferried by the breeze were scattered about. It was clear that the scrapbook activity was a frequent one. Task completed, she then tucked the scissors back into a bag that also concealed a shiv. Catherine felt a certain sense of comfort and preparedness when she had her shiv at hand. Her military background had made her adept at it, and she had never stopped carrying one, even after leaving the service.
"Catherine?" Winston asked, subtly studying her.
"Yes, that's me," Catherine responded without trying to read into his intent.
"You were in the military, right?"

"Correct. Piloting planes wasn't my start." She retorted, the scars of battles both physical and mental marked meditatively on her persona. Indeed, she was an unlikely debtor, having once been highly trained personnel in military combat – the shiv was her preferred weapon, which she'd practiced with consistently after her service days.

Winston noticed the agitation in her eyes as they turned to the topic of Floyd. It was evident Floyd's continuous demand for money had stirred up enough frustration and desperation within Catherine, and the fact that he was planning to take legal action against her only added fuel to the fire.
"Well, Catherine. Nice talking to you," Winston said, standing up from the porch steps. "This is routine, we're talking to everyone Floyd knew."
"Of course, detective. I understand," Catherine said, her rigid military bearing showing through.

As Winston drove away, he couldn't help but replay the entire conversation in his head. Flight or fight. In Catherine’s case, she was always prepared to do either, hence the shiv in her bag. With her financial situation forcing her into a corner, it seemed like fight was becoming her only option.

Winston browsed through the case file while sipping his freshly brewed coffee. The victim, Floyd, was found dead in the library, dead from puncture and cut wounds, potentially from a shiv- an easy enough weapon to make or find.

He sat back in his chair, looking over the CCTV footage from the library. The video stream showed Zara, a local fashion designer known for her extravagant style and equally extravagant temper, walking in and out of the library on the day of the crime. That wouldn't normally place her as a suspect... if it hadn't been for the fact that Floyd and Zara didn't exactly get along.

Floyd had told friends on numerous occasions how Zara had asked him for money, a request he'd always refused. Winston flicked through more notes - Zara had been spending a frightening amount of money on drugs, and her erratic behavior had seen her lose more than one important contract.

He clicked his pen thoughtfully. Zara was well-known for her intricate designs and elaborate fabric work, often using scissors and needles, objects commonly found in her toolkit. It didn't take a seasoned detective to figure out that, with enough motivation, any of these objects could be easily reshaped into a makeshift weapon.

Winston took another sip of his coffee, rubbing his temples. He looked again at the CCTV recording of Zara. She seemed on edge, showing the typical nervous energy of someone under the influence of drugs. He remembered Zara from a case a year ago- a dispute with a rival designer. She had improved her status in the fashion industry immensely since then, but her life clearly had a negative twist.

The library had been filled with people the day Floyd was murdered. Zara, on five separate occasions, was caught on the CCTV entering and exiting the library. Floyd was no different, he also spent a majority of his day there, lost between the shelves of literature. Winston thought back to his initial conversation with his colleagues about the case: something didn't feel right.
"You said Zara often works with sharp tools, right?" Winston asked the officer taking notes.
"Yes, scissors, needles... she says they give her the precision she needs for her work." The officer replied, looking up from her notepad.
Winston knew he had a long day of investigating ahead. With one last glance at the CCTV footage, he left his office prepared to find the truth.

rounds.evidence_text: In the heart of a labyrinth, Samuel lay lifeless, a corkscrew marking his end, throwing Detective Winston into a twisted web of clues, suspects, and secrets.

Winston found himself standing before the grand old labyrinth, a strange sense of nervous excitement bubbling up within him. His next lead, Rachel, had been seen here with the late Samuel not too long ago.
Winston adjusted his hat and proceeded towards the labyrinth's house. According to the intel he had received, Rachel was a tenant and he needed to dig deeper.
As he was led through the maze-like building, Rachel's familiarity with the structure was made clear to him. She had free access, considering her status as a tenant.

In the grand living room of the labyrinth, he spotted a collection of many intricate corkscrews casually displayed in a glass cabinet. The officer who had briefed him had mentioned Rachel's eclectic collection, her acknowledged ability to open wine bottles with one and her reputation as a sommelier; a mastery which requires a sophisticated expertise with corkscrews.

Later, as Winston requested an opportunity to talk, Rachel's past encounters with the law were addressed. She had been in cuffs before on account of murder and the homicide detectives at the station had previously linked several victims to Rachel’s unique pattern of killing—using a corkscrew as a weapon, a pattern that was too specific to belong to anyone else but her.

Just as Winston was about to cut through to the quick, he noticed a piece of paper in the corner of Rachel's otherwise neat room. Peering closer, he spotted Samuel's name at the top of the list. It was confirmed - Samuel was on Rachel's list of confirmed victims that matched her cruel corkscrew method.

Then came the disturbing facts; the ones that didn't sit right with Winston. Among them was the undeniable likeness of poor Samuel to Rachel's former victims. Matching to the tee, in fact, to the known victims, who all bore the mark of her corkscrew.
"Samuel was last seen here, wasn't he?" Winston asked, which Rachel confirmed. She also admitted that they had entered the labyrinth together.

But the most chilling revelation for Winston was the fact that no one else was known to have been in the labyrinth. It was just them, Samuel and Rachel. The isolation within the labyrinth had always made it a place of mystery and unease. It was as if the labyrinth in itself was involved in the elaborate dance of death.

As he departed, Winston wondered why an otherwise forty-something pleasant woman like Rachel, a reputed sommelier, would resort to such chilling activities. But that was the puzzle to solve; the reason for his dogged pursuit of the truth.

Detective Winston leaned against the marble labyrinth walls, picturing the lost Samuel stumbling through, only to find his demise. There was always something eerie about labyrinths. They were designed to lose you. Now, they seemed to encapsulate the mystery that lay before him.

Walking away from the labyrinth, he climbed back into his trusty black Sedan and guided it to Charlotte's studio. He had been told by his colleagues about Charlotte, the celebrated local choreographer. She was reportedly seen distinctively in public places such as shopping malls and parks, with a notepad in her hand, staining the pages fervently as she observed the natural movements of the people around her. She would practice her noted movements again and again until she perfected them for her choreographies.

She wasn't just famous in the artistic locale of the town, but also a known face in the numerous wine-tasting events around. Her appreciation for fine wine, as was apparent by her regular visits to these soirees, added to her persona. Many would see her, savoring the flavor, discussing the notes and delicacies of the fermented grapes. That's what made her request for him to bring a bottle of red wine in their next meeting less surprising.

The studio was buzzing as Winston entered. Charlotte was delicately supervising her dancers, commanding the room with a certain grace. As the bass-heavy music dwindled down, he seized the opportunity to gain her attention. “Charlotte?” Winston introduced himself.

"Detective, please do go ahead and sit," Charlotte gestured, quickly excusing herself to handle a delivery that had just arrived. She opened boxes and packages with a certain familiarity, not unusual for someone who received ample parcels daily. What caught his attention; however, was that she was using a corkscrew to slice open the packages. Uncouth, but practical in some way. Never in his line of work had he seen a corkscrew as a package opener.

As Winston conversed with Charlotte, her defiant love for her sister became evident. There was an uncomfortable history with Samuel where Charlotte's sister played the victim to his harassments. Winston could see the furious protectiveness in Charlotte's eyes as she spoke about her sister's distress under Samuel's provocations

"We have had this conversation before, Detective," Charlotte perched herself on a stool, her excitement dimming into a serious frown. "I confronted Samuel multiple times about his behavior, and I am not shy about arguing for my sister's protection.”
Her ogle darted around the room before landing back on Winston, glossier. “Can we change the subject?” she pleaded. Sensing her growing discomfort, he agreed and asked about her choreography instead.

“Ah, that’s one of my favorite topics!” She sighed happily, reminiscent of a fine wine savant in a tasting session. "I observe people's movements in different public places like malls, parks, and even wine-tasting events. I take notes, try them out multiple times until they feel right and incorporate them into my routines. It’s like I’m borrowing from the world and making something beautiful of it,” Her face glowed with dedication, shadowed by an uneasy sadness.

As Winston prepared to exit the studio, Charlotte requested him for a favor. “Detective, next time you come here, bring a bottle of red along?” A smile painted her lips, gleaming eyes suggesting an implied twinship between the detective and the world of fine wine. “Consider it my fee for the trouble,” she added, chortling softly, her eyes dewy.

As Winston drove away, he remembered her passion carefully stored in the paper-notes, her love for movements and her wines, and her fiery protection towards her sister. The labyrinth seemed a little less daunting now. Not every turn would lead to a path out, but it was a start.

rounds.evidence_text: In the quiet seclusion of a chalet, Mackenzie met her untimely end by a sickle's cruel bite, leaving Detective Winston with two suspects and a chilling mystery to unravel.

Detective Winston froze to make sure there was no crunching beneath his boots as he treaded along the pine needle covered path to the chalet, hiding any indication of his presence. He was there to have a word with Julius, a Rabbi frequenting the chalet for religious gatherings, who'd been seen at the place not once, but twice on the day of the murder. It was, interestingly, the same day that Julius was seen carrying his sickle for religious rituals at his early morning visit.

The door of the chalet swung open on creaking hinges to reveal the tall figure of Julius, adorned in his traditional clothing. "Detective," Julius greeted him, the same sickle he had earlier in the day- used specifically in Jewish religious rituals- hung on the wall behind him; a twin to the one that had ended Mackenzie's life.

"Julius, I'm here to ask you a few questions," Winston began, his eyes drifting to the small blade hanging behind the man. Julius nodded in understanding, stepping aside to allow the detective to enter.

The inside of the chalet was immaculate, all looked as though it was in its appropriate place, nothing before the detective indicated any form of struggle. As they walked deeper into the chalet, Julius spoke to him, "I was wondering when you'd come around, detective. rounds.evidence_text: In the ominous arena of a wrestling ring, Sophie's life was unexpected cut short by the deadly crack of a pistol; now it's up to grizzled Detective Winston to interrogate suspects Willard and Miles, unmasking the murderer among them.

Beside the main floor was a separate storage area, cleverly concealed and invisible from the sales floor - tucked away in a quiet corner where no customer could see. Salesmen were bustling about, attempting to close deals and lure in unsuspecting customers. His gaze settled on a particular man, who was rather keenly explaining the mileage of a specific model to a customer: Miles.
"Mr. Miles," Winston greeted in his stern tone, interrupting the technical talk about mileage.
"Sorry, sir. I'm deep in a conversation," he said, not looking up from the customer.
"I believe this is more important," Winston replied, flashing his badge.

Miles made an excuse to the customer and led Winston toward the hidden storage room, away from the prying eyes of the staff and customers. Entering the secretive area that no other employee had set foot in, Miles seemed visibly unnerved, surrounded by nothing but stacks of tires and car parts.
"Is there something wrong, detective?" He asked, subtly glancing at the locked door behind him.
"Miles, I want to talk to you about Sophie. I understand you were both in the wrestling match. Quite the tough opponent you had there." Winston began.
Miles cleared his throat, "Well, we were more than just opponents in the ring. We've had our issues politically too."
"I'm aware," Winston said curtly, noticing Miles turning defensive.
"Sophie possessed evidence against you, she found out about money laundering carried out through this dealership, perhaps?" Winston probed.
Miles shifted uncomfortably; his complexion changed and he cast his eyes down nervously. "I...I don't know what you're talking about, Detective."
Winston sternly replied, "Sophie planned to reveal these illegal acts. You knew it, didn’t you? She was about to expose your whole operation.”
"Anyone would want to protect their livelihood, Detective,” retorted Miles, avoiding Winston's piercing gaze.
"I see," Winston said calmly assessing the situation, "It seems no one else knows what you do in this storage room Miles."
“Well, it's my dealership, my storage. Do I need an audience now?" Miles retorted, frustration creeping into his voice.
Deciding to change gears a bit, Winston asked, "Say, Miles, you sponsor anyone in Sophie's campaign?"
"Actually I do, I have been secretly financing a competing candidate in Sophie's campaign." Revealed Miles with a mischievous grin, sensing no immediate danger.
"Ah, hedging your bets, are we?" Winston concluded.

"Interesting," Winston said, ending the conversation. He finished up his lukewarm coffee, thanked Mr. Miles for his time, and walked out of the concealed storage room, leaving Miles behind in the stuffy room of tires and car parts.

As he meandered through the dealership, Winston thought about what Miles had said and not said. He stepped out into the parking lot, squinting against the harsh afternoon sun. He had a mystery to solve, and every lead mattered.

Winston took another sip from his coffee cup as he shuffled through the files, his tired eyes narrowing on the name Willard, the initial suspect for the recent wrestling ring homicide. Sophie's death had hit the community like a brick wall, and the press swarmed around it like flies.

Sophie, a champion wrestler, was shot in the ring while performing one of her signature moves. The chaos of that night was still reported in the tabloids, time seemed to have stopped, and the investigation was now up to him.

Sophie had falsely accused Willard of malpractice, however, she won the court case. It was an incident that was the talk of the town. The accusations, though false, were ratified by court, leaving Willard's career as a chiropractor on thin ice. Winston remembered Willard's hands shaking at the courthouse, his eyes burning with something Winston could not quite pinpoint.

Spotting Willard's front-row wrestling event ticket in the collected evidence file, Winston knew he had been there right at the heart of the event. It was well known that mandatory check-ins were required for attendees and part of Willard’s check-in document showed his presence at the entrance of the arena, confirming his presence at that fateful match.

The interviews had a common thread - Willard frequented the wrestling matches. Winston had found the receipts and tickets for each event annotated in Willard's handwriting; it was an unquestionable fact.

Dr. Willard's profile drew Winston's attention. His career as a chiropractor not only required him using protective tools like support belts and gloves, but also a familiarity with the human anatomy that would be advantageous in a wrestling match. It was especially Willard’s second career—his military background—that caught Winston’s eye. Winston had heard about Willard's long career in the army. The firearm training he got there pulled him back to the murder.
Poring over reports again, Winston recalled that Willard carried a firearm for protection. The firearm was engraved into the case's backbone, another undeniable fact that Winston had to grapple with.
He took a deep breath and decided to pay Willard a visit.

Meeting Willard at his office, Winston perched himself on the edge of the chiropractic table, looking at the protective gloves and belts hanging on the wall, it was evident that his chiropractic practice required these safety tools. Winston could see Willard's tension, the hint of uncontrollable worry seeping from his face. He handed over his business card to Willard.
"So, Willard, you were at the wrestling match the night Sophie was shot?" Winston asked.
Willard nodded, "Yes, I was there... I... I usually go to watch the matches. I had a front-row ticket."
Winston opened his notepad, marking it down. "The court case, it was... tough on you, wasn't it?" He asked.
Willard swallowed, nodding again without a word.

Winston stood up to leave, passing a quick glance over the firearms manual lying on the shelf, and pocketed his notepad. He didn't know if he had all the answers, but he was determined to find the truth.

Despite the clear unease on his face, Wilfred sputtered, “I… I… That's impossible. I… I can prove my whereabouts.”

“Well, Sir" Winston said, shifting slightly to reveal the mall’s security camera pointing directly at them, "you may have to explain why you, Mr. Wilfred, have been spotted on our CCTV not too long ago, roughly at the same time Xenia was found murdered. "And were you at the rink when this all transpired?" He asked steering back to the line of questioning.
"Most of the day, yes." Yvette confirmed. "I was there for the initial setup and Justin was there too."

Yvette had seen an early draft of the revealing speech herself.
"Did the speech upset you, Yvette?" He asked, wrapping up his interrogation.
"What can I say detective, people have opinions," Yvette defended, "I just try to focus on my work."

Engagements done for the day, detective Winston made his way back to the precinct. Another puzzle to solve, another murderer to catch; the game was beginning. He had a feeling it was going to be a long night.

Stacks of paperwork about the latest crime related to a high-profile hockey player, Justin, lay across Winston’s desk. Retirement had been just around the corner for Justin but his life was cut short and the hockey rink, ironically, had witnessed his curtain fall. His team had been under a dark cloud of continuous defeat recently.

Lillian looked up from her reverie, "Yes, that's correct," she responded, her gaze drifting back to the locket.

Winston’s eyes darted to the locket, noted, and quickly moved away. He dug out the files about Lillian's background. Lillian had frequently disclosed amongst her circle of friends that she passionately coveted the captain's position.

Nurse Emma appeared aloof, "Trust me, I've tried to make a conversation with her. She mostly stays quiet, lost in her locket."

Winston looked at Lillian, her head bowed low, avoiding any eye contact just like she did in her group sessions, according to the other patients.

"Yes, I did want that..." her voice trailed away, "I believe I would have done a good job." Her tone dripped with contempt and displeasure towards Justin's power.

The events of the day already earned a special notation in his mental files. Silently, Detective Winston drove back towards the precinct, a storm of thoughts racing as swiftly as his accelerating car. He knew this was just the beginning of a path penned with enigmas.
