rounds.evidence_text: In the neon-lit labyrinth of a local jazz club, the melody of intrigue rises as Detective Winston interrogates Gregory and Madelyn following the fatal twist of a dagger finding home in Abigail's heart.

Winston sat quietly, eyes closed as the melodic tunes of the jazz band echoed around the club. This was the last place Abigail had been alive, an exciting and lively jazz club just around the block from the auction house. Gregory often found solace in the live music after a long day of auctioneering.

This was not exactly how Winston had pictured an auctioneer — the eccentric hairstyles and the ever-changing eye color almost seemed out of place. It was a trendy hair salon, where Gregory was seen frequently, the very place where he picked up the hottest hairstyle every week.

As the auction closed, Gregory was seen stepping out from the auction house appearing somewhat relieved. Revenge in the air as Abigail had been on the edge of revealing a secret that would cripple Gregory's career as an auctioneer forever. The quiet murmurs of the patrons in the auction hall only escalating the tension.

Winston ventured towards the auction house the following day. As the day turned into evening, Gregory arrived carrying a small bag. He was approached by the security guard who nodded in recognition, allowing the auctioneer inside with no questions asked. So, Gregory indeed had access to the auction house and its collections after hours.

Winston found himself hovering around the dagger collection. One in particular caught his eye, it was remarkably similar to the one used to murder Abigail. Gregory had auctioned a similar one on the night of the murder.

He contemplated this later walking down the street, passing a storefront when something caught his eye. It was a small shop selling colored contacts. Looking at the CCTV footage, Winston recognized Gregory purchasing some colored contacts at the store. And just like his trendy hairstyles, Gregory's eye color seemed to change every few days.
As the evening deepened, Gregory was seen leaving the auction house and stepping into the jazz club. The same sequence of events that had taken place on the night of Abigail's murder.
"Mister Gregory, can I have a word with you?" Winston approached the auctioneer later that night, finding him in the dimly lit jazz club. Gregory accepted with a nod.
"So, you're a frequenter, I heard?" Winston made lighthearted conversation.
"Only after each auction, detective." Gregory answered coolly. No signs of guilt, only a man enjoying his evening with his familiar jazz music.
"Must be nice, being an auctioneer, seeing all sorts of precious things come and go."
Gregory chuckled, "Quite so, detective. Keeps the job exciting."
"And the jazz club, just around the corner. Convenient, isn't it?”
“Indeed,” Gregory concluded cryptically. Winston left him at that, gathering his coat and calling it a night. There was some catching up to do and a murderer to catch.

Winston turned the crime scene photos over and over in his mind. The jazz club was bustling, alive with music, laughter, and the chatter of living souls. Between the shadowy saxophone player and the wisps of smoky haze, the rolling melodies echoed cries for the one lost – Abigail.

Winston sighed and rose from his chair, reaching for his coat. In one corner of the crime scene picture, a glimmering dagger caught his eye, a seemingly misplaced relic amidst the modern jazz club surroundings. With an imminent late-night visit to the scene, he prepared for his encounter with Madelyn.
Arriving at Madelyn's office after her return from a late-night meeting across town, he waited patiently as she packed her files into a briefcase, still working after a long day.
"Busy day?" He asked, glancing at her overflowing case.

"Always is, Detective - high-conflict cases aren't known for their simplicity. Goes with the territory I suppose, and constant travelling to take care of these cases, of course,", she sighed, heaving her bag onto her shoulder and motioning for Winston to follow her towards the elevator.
In the limbo between floors, Winston studied Madelyn. The fine lines creasing her forehead and the dull tiredness in her eyes spoke volumes of late nights in the office and constant travelling.
"Coffee?" She asked, sitting heavily into her chair in the dimly lit room, motioning to a nearby coffee pot.
"No thanks, just want to be clear on some things," Winston said, refusing the siren call of caffeine.
"On that dagger incident, you mean? It's an antique from my collection. Some kind of sick joke, I suppose."
"Niche hobby, isn't it?" Winston remarked calmly.
"History unfolds with every piece from the past – it's actually quite intriguing if you take the time to dive in," she replied, looking beyond Winston into her past with a distant gaze.

Conversation shifted to the late Abigail with a heavy tone, feeling more like a performance than genuine grief. Madelyn bitterly explained how the two of them used to be good friends until they fell out over a huge debt she unfortunately borrowed from Abigail.

"She was threatening to drag me to the court and make my debt public... Just imagine the public humiliation, " she confessed with a shake of the head, her eyes reflecting a mixture of resentment and fear. "And let’s not forget that winning lawsuit could’ve spelled financial ruin for me. It terrified me."

In the quiet of her office, the soft ticking of the clock echoed with each second. The room absorbed her words, casually dancing around the real question Winston was going to ask. Just as he was about to probe further, a distant melody caught his ear. The melody spelt jazz and Madelyn noticed his interest.

"The club? Oh, it's just about 10 minutes from here. I can hear them sometimes when I work late, or when I return from late-night meetings." Madelyn said, almost wistful. The jazz notes from distance seemed to play a mournful tribute for the late Abigail as Winston thanked Madelyn for her time and left her office.

rounds.evidence_text: In a seedy motel room, Frederick's life was cruelly punctuated with a corkscrew, leaving Detective Winston to unravel the twisted tales of two suspects, Tessa and Van.

Winston's dispatch message included the name "Tessa". He remembered her as a skilled bartender at a high-end restaurant, famed for her unique way of handling a corkscrew, especially while opening extravagant wine bottles. Recently, she seemed to have been working outside of normal working hours. She was often seen requesting financial support from Frederick, an affluent regular customer who wouldn't mind doling out his means for attention.

A friend once mentioned to him Frederick’s intention to spill the beans about Tessa's grim reality. It was not every day someone aimed to settle a debt of that size, and the situation intrigued Winston. Using the information he had, he traced that Tessa had checked in the motel a couple of days before Frederick’s demise.

Winston pulled his sedan into the dusty lot of the low-rise motel on the outskirts of town. There he saw Tessa, emerging from a room and handing a key back to the motel manager. The motel staff confirmed that the implicating room was indeed paid for by Tessa, and their logbook showed that she had checked in before Frederick’s death. They also agreed that she had remained on the premises throughout.

The day Tessa was arrested, she displayed her usual calm demeanor. As the police handcuffed her, a metallic shine of a corkscrew slipped out from her apron pocket, landing on the ground below. This was her personal corkscrew, a tool she always had on hand for her routine work at the restaurant, and one that she was seen using frequently to open wine bottles during her shift.

As Winston left the motel to return to the precinct, he mused over the victim’s connection with Tessa. Frederick knew about Tessa’s considerable debt, and this was not ordinary behavior between a server and a regular patron. But for now, the facts just laid out the circumstances. His sole contribution to this puzzle would be to compile the facts so they could make sense. The rest — the swift execution of justice — was a matter of time. And Winston knew that time always brought the truth to light.

Winston straightened his tie as he approached the scene of Frederick's murder, squinting under the motel's harsh fluorescent lighting. Frederick, a successful events planner, was stealing lucrative contracts right from Van’s territory. On the other hand, Van also managed to poach a few of Frederick's prime clients. Frederick's competitors saw his success as the rising spark of a problem they had to deal with. Someone like Van, maybe.

Van. The one who was always behind a desk at every event he planned, for some reason avoiding any kind of physical exertion. For instance, at every event, he could be found refusing a spot in the robust, physically-demanding relay races that colleagues customarily participated in. That night was no different, the event was a wine tasting. Van would likely be there, not participating in the traditional grape-stomping competition. There, Van would flaunt his newly-acquired clients; the ones he had usurped from Frederick.

With this thought in his head, Winston drove over to the event, arriving to the sight of Van pouring wine expediently with a corkscrew for the event attendees instead of joining in on the active games.
"Van," Winston greeted, nodding at him.
"Detective," Van replied, raising an eyebrow.
He paused as Winston took a seat in front of him, then offered a bottle of red. "Wine, Detective?"
"No, thanks," Winston said, "Don't you usually have an assistant to open wine bottles?"
Van laughed, shrugging off the observation easily. "I like doing it. It's therapeutic," he said.

Then there was the fresh dressing peeking out from under Van's cuff, the one he offered some vague explanation for, just like every other time Winston had seen him injured. He referred to these as ‘small accidents’.
He remembered what Van's colleagues had said about him. Always getting injured, never playing in any games, always behind a desk, and there was that thing with Frederick.
"Frederick," Winston started, both men looking somber at the mention of the recent murder. Van averted his gaze, focusing steadfastly on the bottle he was opening.
"I heard you had a falling out."

Van sighed, and for the first time that evening he looked tired. "Fred and I... we had our differences. He was snatching clients right under my nose. And I wasn't just taking it lying down, I got back at him by snatching some of his clients,” he confessed.
"Heard you even threatened him once," Winston said quietly.
"That was just business, nothing personal," Van replied coldly. "If you're suggesting--"
Winston lifted his hands, chuckling lightly. "I'm not suggesting anything, Van," he said carefully.

Turning his attention back to the bottle, Van popped the cork and poured himself a glass. "Fine. I had my disagreements with Frederick," he admitted. "Yes, we threatened each other over clients. But that's all it was... just threats."

Winston left shortly after, leaving Van to his wine and his thoughts. As he walked back to the car, he remembered the coroner's report. Those puncture wounds in Frederick's autopsy. Consistent with a corkscrew...
A steady cold rain fell on Winston's windshield as he drove away, leaving behind the warm lights of the wine tasting event and a man with a lot on his mind.

rounds.evidence_text: In the dim light of an abandoned factory, Kaylee's lifeless body lay with the cold steel of a pickaxe lodged within, thrusting Detective Winston into a dark game of deception with suspects Penelope and Francis.

Winston breathed a sigh of relief as he entered the comfort of his car, escaping the oppressive heat outside. The day had been anything but a usual one and he reviewed the paper on his clipboard yet again. Kaylee, a young woman, was found dead in an abandoned factory of all places and the purported weapon was a pickaxe, an old miner's pickaxe to be exact.

His next interview was scheduled with a nanny named Penelope. Penelope was not your average nanny. Alongside her formal education in early child care, she also had professional training in the same field, acquiring skills that allowed her to excel in handling children. Despite her credible qualifications, Winston found it decidedly strange to connect a nanny with such a gruesome find, not least because Penelope herself had most of her busy day spent with children, not in an old factory.
After a short walk, he approached a modest suburban home quite close to the abandoned factory. The home itself, despite its proximity, seemed worlds apart from the grim discovery location.

Penelope greeted him at the door, shaking his hand with a warm smile. "Hello, Penelope." Winston greeted, then a thought hit him. A person of her profession is typically responsible for a child's growth and upbringing. Penelope's studied and trained background in childcare had indeed stuck in his mind since their last encounter.

During their conversation, Winston learned that Penelope was seen leaving her house around the estimated time of the murder. Interestingly enough, he even had a witness claiming to see Penelope with an old mining pickaxe earlier that day, a claim solidly backed up as the recovered pickaxe, the very same weapon used in the murder, matched exactly the one described by the witness.

Just as he was thinking about the pickaxe, a piece of evidence from the crime scene flashed across his mind. Winston reached into his jacket pocket to pull out a page from a diary. It was from Kaylee's diary. The entry was clear; Kaylee had a meeting scheduled with Penelope at the so-called abandoned factory.

A unease washed over Winston, making the usually delicious coffee taste sour in his mouth. Kaylee seemed to have known something about Penelope that she didn't want public. She had unearthed something about Penelope's past... maybe even criminal past. The parents didn't know... and Kaylee was planning to tell.

He glanced at Penelope, who was sitting across from him, looking anxious. She must've known that the exposure would cause her serious embarrassment... and at worst, cost her her job. With no other events reported that could have prevented Kaylee from meeting Penelope, it all looped back to the meeting at the factory.

"Well, Penelope, I do have a long walk back to my car." he said, finishing the last of his coffee and standing up. "I've taken enough of your time, thank you for your cooperation." He gave a nod as he reached the door, leaving the nanny to contemplate her day filled with children, and his with unanswered questions.

Detective Winston grimaced, finally setting down the carefully documented police case file of the late Kaylee. The coffee stains on the file folder began to bleed into the corners of the cover. The pangs of guilt for indulging in too much work in the form of an overbrewed cup of joe were not his only concern. An image haunted him; it was from a video footage where Francis had caught Kaylee red-handed, threatening his daughter which he digitally recorded as proof.

Shaking the sudden chill from his spine, Winston looked out of his office window to the abandoned factory where Kaylee had been found. Francis, Kaylee's husband, had years of mining experience and was renowned for his pickaxe expertise. Francis had arranged the meeting point and was seen coaxing her into trusting that the factory would be undisturbed.

The town had all been abuzz with this unthinkable murder. Kaylee's constant torment of Francis' daughter, enough to induce anxiety and depression in the child, was now common knowledge. Even more upsetting was the unusual delicateness Francis had shown in handling this situation, a man known for his work involving grueling physical labor that required a high level of strength and endurance.

Digging into his pocket Winston pulled out the receipt for the pickaxe that he'd found in Francis’ pocket, a peculiar coincidence considering Francis’ mining background and the tool associated with it.

In the corner of his foul-smelling, second-hand leather bound desk was a photograph. A crisp, clear frame showing Francis purchasing the said pickaxe at the local hardware store. It was not surprising that Francis had chosen to arm himself with a tool he was already so familiar with, but to invite his wife into a murderous trap of his creation was another level of distressing reality.
Winston looked up to see Francis standing in the doorway, tall and solemn. "Detective Winston," he said quietly, "We need to talk about Kaylee."
Winston nodded, gesturing for him to take a seat. "I heard about what happened. About the threats she made to your daughter."
Francis looked taken aback, his gaze shifting around the room. "Yes...I caught her threatening our daughter. I don't know why she couldn't see what her actions were doing to our daughter."

Winston nodded but said nothing. He stayed silent, letting Francis explain in his own time, about the factory meeting he'd arranged with Kaylee, his knowledge that the factory would have been empty at that time, the purchased pickaxe and the chilling threats Kaylee had aimed towards his daughter.
As Francis left his office, Winston glanced back at the file, picking up the coffee cup, he pondered the gritty mysteries life tended to serve up.

rounds.evidence_text: In the haunting echoes of a cinema hall, Tracy's life was abruptly silenced by the grim stroke of a meat cleaver, leaving Detective Winston grappling with a chilling mystery and two elusive suspects - Nicole and Gloria.

Winston, standing behind the caution tape, looked at the cinema marquee. He allowed the scene to imprint itself in his mind before he would venture inside to inspect the crime scene. A murder at the movies was a rarity. But what was even more unusual was the murder weapon used: a meat cleaver.

Reviewing the details of the case once more, Winston thought about some key players involved. Undeniably traceable was Gloria, a hardcore fan of the rock band 'The Butchers', known by everyone and even herself in interviews, as a groupie. She had also confessed in one such media interaction that she was crazy about taxidermy, a hobby brought to life in her house.

From the ceiling to the floor, taxidermied animals filled the house with glassy eyes reflecting in the dim light, a testimony to her hobby.
Among her collection, he noticed a recent addition - a rare bird, its exotic colors momentarily catching his gaze. Bob, the local bird dealer, had already confirmed its purchase by Gloria.

"Well, I was at the movie premiere, of course," Gloria responded. "I, along with Tracy, went to the double event. The Butchers premiered their new music video during the movie. And well, you couldn't expect me to miss that, now could you? I follow every event they put up and not just because I'm a fan. Because I am in love with the lead singer, and yes I'm saying it."
Winston let the information sink in.
"Well... isn't it true that Tracy, the victim, was planning to go public with an affair?" Winston asked.
A momentary flicker passed in Gloria's eyes. "Yes... I know about that," Gloria confessed. "She was dating the lead singer, the poor man. She wanted to reveal everything, destroy everything."

With that, Winston left Gloria's house with more questions buzzing in his head. He got back into his car, piecing together the intricate web of clues this case held. The concert that the Butchers were supposed to play after the movie was now going to be remembered for all the wrong reasons.

Deep in thought, Winston flipped through the photographs of the movie theatre crime scene, when his partner handed him an envelope. A DVD from the theatre's CCTV records, witnessing every unscripted moment at the theatre that did double-duty, not just as a place to showcase films, but also as a distinctive setting for unorthodox weddings, just like the one Tracy had intended to have. Eyewitnesses at the scene confirmed Nicole's presence at the theatre during the murder. The records would be viewed later.

His current priority was to interrogate Nicole, the esteemed wedding planner, the woman whose entire reputation and business were built on her success in this field. By an unfortunate coincidence, she had been at the theatre when Tracy was murdered, not just as a cinema enthusiast, but as the individual orchestrating Tracy's movie-themed wedding at the same theatre.
"Nice place you've got here," Winston observed as he ventured into Nicole's office, its grandeur coupled with an array of movie posters illustrating her success in planning film-themed weddings.
"Well, Detective, events won't plan themselves," Nicole said, with a small, tight smile. "Tracy hired me for one of my elaborate movie-themed weddings. She was drawn to the unusual."

Surveying the space, he noticed it was not only amassed with wedding supplies but also held a vast array of kitchen equipment. Nicole had been responsible for preparing the meat at several events as evident from the professional cleavers that took center stage amongst the kitchenware. One of them catching his eye; a meat cleaver.
"On food responsibility as well?" Winston asked.

"Indeed. Delivering comprehensive experiences is the goal. Every specification matters, including the banquet," Nicole imparted. "My past as a culinary student till being a wedding planner helped shape that. I even received professional training in meat preparation."
"Interesting," Winston murmured, quickly connecting two points - Nicole's past culinary training and Tracy's murder weapon, a meat cleaver.
"Rumor has it that you made a considerable blunder at Tracy's wedding," Winston broached. "Word on the street is that Tracy was so embarrassed she was looking to file a malpractice suit against you.”
"A minor miscalculation. No one is perfect, detective. However, Tracy blew it out of proportion," Nicole responded, her face growing somber.

Observing her seemingly unflustered demeanor, Winston mused on her case. He knew a large scale malpractice suit could irreparably harm a professional's reputation. For someone like Nicole whose entire business relied on her successful track record as a wedding planner, it could be a fateful blow.

Before confronting her head-on, he decided to examine the perspectives of the eyewitnesses and the CCTV footage. His eyes strayed to the cold, gleaming steel of the meat cleaver amidst Nicole's kitchen equipment. This reminded him of Tracy, and he made himself a promise: he would find justice for her.

In the haze of flashing lights and the flurry of police activity, Detective Winston found himself reflecting on the scene before him— a once lively session of travel had turned into a horrifying crime scene. Keira, an acclaimed actress, met a gruesome end somewhere above the clouds within the confines of an airplane.

He peered at the seating plan. Keira and a certain makeup-artist, Roy, had been ensconced close to each other. Roy's profession intrigued Winston. Being a makeup artist, Roy had open access to the movie props. In his regular line of duty, he had even been responsible for the movie props. Winston quietly wondered how Roy felt about handling props so deadly. The movie currently in production, as Winston learned, even had a sequence where a shotgun was fired. Apart from props, though, Roy was qualified to handle guns. The knowledge made Winston's eyes narrow, and a sense of unease lingered in the air.

Winston turned his attention to the individual interviews. Part of his job, however unappealing. He questioned Roy's social circle, most of which agreed to having seen Roy use cocaine during parties. Even a casual search of his wallet at the scene had brought Winston into contact with traces of cocaine on Roy's dollar bills.

As the evening drew closer to the end, a haunting stillness took hold over the airplane as Winston took notes, suitably filed away with an enigmatic makeup artist named Roy.

As Detective Winston sat in the bustling airport terminal, he couldn't shake the feeling that he had entered into a scene straight out of a soap opera. Keira, the victim, had been brutally shot on an airplane mid-flight. It beggared belief but, somehow, it weirdly made the situation even more intriguing, albeit less appealing.

On one side of the investigation was Angela, a woman who had ties everywhere – friend, confidante, protector, and presently, a suspect. Their history ran deep. "You Adam?" asked Winston, walking towards him.

rounds.evidence_text: In an adrenaline inducing bungee jumping site, Mack's thrill-seeking adventure came to a gruesome end by a nunchaku; now, it's up to Detective Winston to unravel the deadly secrets between Mackenzie and Ana.

Winston nodded, making a mental note of Mackenzie's reaction. They turned the conversation to martial arts and during the chat, Mackenzie unintentionally revealed their prowess with nunchaku.

Ridicule. That was a word Winston had already heard before concerning Mack. He asked around, among their friends, everyone said the same, Mack liked to joke, to point fun at beliefs. Especially Ana’s it seemed.

They left together, Ana and Mack, the morning of the murder, people had seen them. Winston asked why, given their strained relationship. Ana shrugged off, her hands trembling. “He wasn’t too bad,” she replied.

Nobody else was documented at the bungee jumping site that day, only Mack and Ana. It was time to head there. Winston thanked Ana for her time and left, driving straight to the scene. He stared up at the looming diving board, picturing the scene.

"Howdy, Miss. I'm Detective Winston. Can I talk with you for a moment?"

"You're here about Ana, aren't you?"

In her voice, Winston heard the threads of grief, but underneath it all was a tangible hint of obsession. According to her friends, talking about Ana was Bethany's habitual way of coping. Bethany's story was compelling, from her military background to her serving duties at the local base, known for its hefty supply of grenades - a dangerous knowledge she was specifically trained for.
"Yes, about Ana... It must have been hard for you. I heard you two were close."

Bethany's face scrunched at that. "Close? Ana was... she was everything to me. I told her as much. But she... she just saw me as a friend." She added the last bit in so softly, Winston had to incline his head to hear.
Trying to divert from the topic, he commented. "That was a good game you played back there. You and Ana... same team I presume?"

"You could say that," she replied grinning. "All of us were here, in the very same game, believing that it's just another fun day. Though Ana was always the one who wanted to win. I even followed her around everywhere to learn how she played."
Winston glanced at his watch. The time of the paintball game coincided with the exact time when Ana was found. A chilling coincidence he couldn't ignore.

As he turned to leave, Bethany called out one last thing.
"Detective Winston? We all loved Ana... Some of us more than others."
As Winston walked towards his car, his mind replayed those words over and over again. It was just another piece of the puzzle... and another step closer to finding out what really happened to Ana.

"Salvador?"
"Yeah, that's me," he replied, wiping sweat from his brow.
Winston motioned to a nearby bench. "Do you mind if we chat for a few moments?"
Salvador glanced at his watch. "Sure, I've got a few minutes."
They sat.
"Nice day out, isn't it?" Canvasing the area, Winston's eyes landed on a small poster. The image was of a verdant campground, similar to the one where Hugo was killed. "You like camping, Salvador?"
Salvador, caught off guard, blinked. "Yes, I do. I go regularly, whenever I can... even to that campground over there".

They chatted about the great outdoors, the joy of being connected with nature, and the complexities of their camping hobbies. Salvador didn’t seem aware that Winston’s questions were leading to anything in particular.
After a few minutes of casual conversation, Winston stood up from the bench. "Thanks for talking with me, Salvador. Nice day, isn't it?"
"Yes, indeed," Salvador replied, stretching his arms. He watched Winston drove away curiously, before shaking his head and walking back to his car.

Winston's next stop was Salvador's house; he observed from a safe distance as Salvador fiddled with something in his garage. Later, when Salvador had retreated into his house, Winston took a closer look under the cover of darkness. He could see an array of axes, various sizes and shapes, displayed proudly on a wall. He saw newly chopped wood stacked neatly in the corner of his backyard, evidence of Salvador’s recent chopping endeavours.

Winston shared his observations with the local police but stepped back after providing his input. They would carry out any necessary searches with legal authorisations while Winston handled the interviews, suspicions and evidence collecting. It was a symbiotic relationship of professional respect.

The puzzling thing nagging at Winston's mind was Hugo's recent decision to stop supplying Salvador with drugs. Something provoked him to cut off Salvador, who was heavily addicted and relied on those supplies. His need was increasing, the gaps between his fixes shortening. Salvador owed Hugo a considerable sum, standing out amidst all the other jumbled pieces.

Whenever Winston asked him about the night of the murder, Salvador always shrugged, a feeble excuse always at the ready, nothing concrete or credible. He didn’t provide any strong alibi for where he was that night. He admitted that he was in the vicinity, at that campground where he regularly camped, but no one witnessed him there. It was clear that Salvador knew how to handle an axe, and there was one found at his place that matched the murder weapon.

Winston knew convictions weren't made on this sort of circumstantial evidence, but there were threads that linked Salvador to the crime scene. There was more groundwork to be done. One thing was certain; Winston wouldn’t stop until justice was served.

rounds.evidence_text: In the quiet of a home office, Mackenzie met a fiery end via a flamethrower, leaving Detective Winston tasked with questioning the two unlikely suspects, Sophia and Virgil.

As Winston closed the victim's office door behind him, he hummed a tune from one of the old tunes he had heard growing up. A home office painted with scorch marks and scars from flames, not the ordinary scene he would walk into. Mackenzie's death was indeed beyond ordinary.

A local artist, Sophia, was on Winston's list for interviews. The name Sophia resonated in the art world, known for her bizarre fire-based creations. Winston remembered; the art reviews had used words like "charred" to describe her artwork. Moreover, he knew that she was often seen transporting flamethrowers to her studio, intriguing the townsfolk. It was said that she used these flamethrowers in her creative process.

Winston found Sophia in her studio, surrounded by antiques that greatly resemble family heirlooms. But he knew this couldn't be the case as both Sophia's mother and sibling had confirmed to him that they did not have possession of any family heirlooms. Therefore, Sophia must have been purchasing these artifacts, and his suspicions were confirmed when he noticed the receipt from a local antique dealer. It was the same dealer who had mentioned that Sophia paid a high price for each item.
"Sophia?" Winston asked, catching the attention of the artist, who had her back to him.
"Yes, that's me," Sophia replied, pushing her disheveled hair behind her ear. Her face was thin and pale. Dark circles hung heavy under her eyes.
"You purchase a lot of antiques, Sophia?" Winston had noticed the receipt and the dealer's confirmation of the high prices.
"Yes, I do," Sophia replied, casting a glance around her at the collected objects. "They're all pretty expensive, but worth the uniqueness they bring to my art."
Winston decided to press about a more sensitive issue. "Mackenzie," he said, and Sophia's expression shifted. "She found your stash, didn't she?"
Sophia’s face paled even further. "No comment," she muttered, but her jittery hands gave her away.

"I understand she had been funding your art and supporting your addiction habit...your addiction, Sophia," Winston added the words slipping past his lips. He revealed how Mackenzie had threatened to cut Sophia off from her art funds unless she got clean and to tell the world about Sophia's addiction if she didn't get help.

Sophia looked away, a flame dancing in her eyes, mirroring the charred elements in her artwork. In those eyes, Winston found a desperate artist drowning in her own addiction and, the financial torment that was coming along with it. A need for money, for drugs.
"Sophia, her threats...you did hear them, didn't you?" Winston's voice was low.
Sophia, barely audible, whispered, "I heard her."

The evidence was there: the futile search for family heirlooms, the expensive antiques, the thinly-veiled threats from Mackenzie, all leading towards an artist struggling with her addiction. An artist desperate for money and lost in her need for drugs.

"Thank you, Sophia," Winston stood from his chair, but before he left, his eyes trained on a flamethrower stored in the corner of the studio. With these parting words, he left, "Take care of yourself, Sophia."

As Detective Winston entered Virgil's home gym, the smell of iron and sweat filled his nostrils. Walls lined with mirrors reflected the image of a man who spent a great deal of time building his formidable strength and size through lifting heavy weights.
"Detective," Virgil called out in a deep, gravelly voice, his muscular arms moving a stacked barbell with almost mechanical precision. "Couldn't help but notice Mackenzie in your stack of files."
"She mentioned you helped her out around her home office. Moving heavy things and such?" Winston questioned, observing Virgil's intense workout regime.
"Helped her plenty, Detective. Many times, she'd call needing my strength." He said, pausing to wipe away the sweat that trickled down his forehead.
"According to witnesses, your last visit to Mackenzie's wasn't so friendly," Winston remarked, his gaze intense, "You were spotted over at Mackenzie's house on the day she was murdered."
Virgil set down the weight he had been lifting and turned to face Winston. "Yes, the witnesses are correct. I was at her house that day, but I swear I didn't kill her." He admitted.

Detective Winston noticed a glass cabinet filled with an assortment of exotic weaponry. Virgil seemed to be someone who appreciated the unusual; the flamethrower that sat amidst the collection was proof of that. Winston's eyes narrowed slightly at the sight of it.
"A flamethrower," He pointed out. "Not something you see every day."
Virgil nodded, his arms crossed over his chest. "I do have a penchant for the extraordinary."
Winston noticed a glaring void on the trophy shelf, amidst the other varied bodybuilding accolites Virgil had accrued. Virgil followed his gaze.
"That's where my prized trophy used to sit. Winning it took an awful lot out of me...quite literally." Virgil's voice betrayed a hint of vulnerability.
"A piece of metal making you this emotional?" Winston asked, looking at the bodybuilder, his brows lifted in feigned curiosity.

"Means a lot more to me than just that, Detective," Virgil was quick to retort, his eyes brimming with a mix of anger and sadness, "Especially after you work hard, and the fruits of that labor are just taken away...stolen and sold off like some trinket."
"Mackenzie did that?" Winston inquired, recalling from the witnesses' statements about her selling Virgil's trophy.
"Sure did, Detective. Laughed in my face about it too. Mocked me for placing such value on it." Virgil’s voice tightened around the final words, raw feelings evident in his gaze.
Winston took a deep breath, processing all the information. "I appreciate your honesty, Virgil. I will be on my way now."
With that, Detective Winston left the brawny bodybuilder standing amidst the mirrored room.

rounds.evidence_text: When fitness enthusiast Rufus was found dead from a hunting knife wound at his local gym, it's up to seasoned Detective Winston to interview top suspects Harvey and Sergio in a baffling murder mystery.
Winston packed up the case files, photographs, and letters into another case file with a heavy sigh. Rufus's case seemed like it was going to be a long one.

He had visited the crime scene, a local fitness center, where Harvey, the primary person of interest, was a regular. It was known that the murder occurred during Harvey's unfalteringly regular workout hours, times that also happened to align perfectly with Rufus's own gym routine.

A local shop owner, a close friend of Harvey and mutual acquaintance of Rufus mentioned in passing that Harvey, despite being a highly trained astronaut with extensive physical and combat training, always insisted on supplementing his intense regimen at his local fitness center. She added how frequently Harvey came by to stock up on protein shakes before his solo routines at the gym.

This was an astronaut who could handle sharp tools skillfully as part of his duty and was never without his trusted hunting knife; it was an integral part of his training kit. Today, she looked worried as she handed over Harvey's preferred protein shake, "He took this from here before his last workout session with... with Rufus."

Feeling the need to prod a bit further, Winston asked her if Harvey had ever mentioned Rufus to her. The woman suddenly hesitated. "Oh... the poor lad looked so disturbed whenever Rufus' name came up. He told me once that Rufus had material on him... That it could ruin him, end his career as an astronaut."

Winston thanked her for her time and made his way to the fitness center. He was led to a locker labelled 'Harvey'; it wasn't locked. Inside, Winston saw an imposing hunting knife, unmistakably an astronaut's tool.

As he looked around, the manager of the fitness center struck up a chat with him, "Harvey... ah yeah, he spends a lot of time here. Always has this intense look, you know? Like he's concentrating real hard on each thing, knife skills and combat included."
"He works out alone," the manager added. "Said it helps him stay focused... He was always on Rufus' schedule though. They worked out together, you know?"

Ruminating over these new insights, Winston decided on his next course of action. It was time to talk to Harvey, to observe him face-to-face, to look for any flicker of recognition, of distress, when Rufus was mentioned.

The halls of the upscale fitness center hummed with an undercurrent of activity. Winston swept his gaze around, looking for one particular face among the hustle and bustle of yoga mats and protein shakes. He had a convincing suspicion that Rufus, the man who was found lifeless at the fitness center only yesterday, did not die of natural causes. He had been at the fitness center the day before, adhered strictly to a fitness routine that Sergio, an introverted masseur, was aware of.

Walking against the flow, he moved towards the isolated rooms touched only by the hands of Sergio, the soundproof massage chambers where clients often noted his silence during sessions. Sergio's reticence extended beyond his work hours, his colleagues could attest to this; they had never seen him at any social event or heard him discuss his personal life with anyone at the gym.

"Sergio," Winston nodded at the stocky, dark-eyed masseur who was lost amidst his silent world. Essentially a man of few words, Sergio was reputed for making his clients comfortable with his calming effect - no prying questions or unnecessary remarks about personal matters or otherwise.

"I've some questions about Rufus," Winston began. He unfolded a schedule from his pocket, Rufus’s regular fitness routine. "You were supposed to have a massage session with him yesterday, the day he was...” He left the sentence trailing. In return, Sergio merely nodded tersely, following his habitual conversation style.

Winston continued, "Rufus noticed your unusual closeness with his wife. I’m sure it wasn’t your intention, but it was enough to make him jealous. He was open about this with a few of his trusted friends."  He watched Sergio's face closely, saw a flicker of emotion. "I understand their relationship threatened to tarnish her reputation, being from such a well-respected, wealthy family, an affair could lead to a scandal."
"N-no, nothing," Sergio stuttered, his face turning pale. His silence had suddenly gained a new edge of discomfort.
"Rufus found a love letter in his wife’s purse, signed by you," Winston said, watching Sergio recoil. The silence deepened in the room, sucking away any remnants of casual conversation.

As Winston left the room, leaving Sergio to mull over his words, he saw a longing in Sergio's gaze. A single tear rolling down his cheeks. "I didn't mean to fall in love with her, but I did. I couldn't bear the idea of losing her," Sergio confessed brokenly, indisputable proof of his deep emotional bond with Rufus’s wife. The love letter, Sergio’s appointment with Rufus, and his unusual familiarity with Rufus’ wife – it was almost as if the pieces of a dark puzzle were slowly falling into place.

rounds.evidence_text: In the heart of a verdant rainforest, Isla had tragically met her end by a lead pipe, prompting Detective Winston to start sifting through the eerie silence, with Jesse and Brian as the prime suspects.

Winston frowned in concentration while browsing through the piles of family photos placed tastefully on a side table at the ceremony.  Isla, the beautiful young woman, was the star in almost every picture. Winston scanned every photo meticulously, but Brian, who had been a janitor for the family for many years, was nowhere to be found.

His attention was diverted from the photographs when the back door of the mortuary creaked open, and Brian stepped in hesitantly. He seemed self-conscious about his tardiness, his back hunched and his gaze darting around the room. Winston glanced over at the service in progress. Brian wasn’t mentioned as a friend or a relative during the service, but he stayed until the end of the burial, lingering as the crowd started to disperse. His aloof demeanor piqued Winston’s interest.

The next day found Winston scanning the tools in Brian's workspace. As per his janitorial duties, Brian handled an assortment of tools, the most common of which were lead pipes. His workspace deep in the jungle revealed that he had been working there for many years, in fact, over a decade, blending his job with nature, dirt, and rust.

Winston remembered that a witness had seen Brian cleaning in the rainforest, a lead pipe in hand, on the same day Isla’s body was discovered. Brian was probably mending a burst pipe he had mentioned to Winston during a casual conversation. The rainforest, where Isla had been brutally murdered, was - oddly enough - a second home to Brian. Rainforest cleaning sounded strange to Winston but perhaps that was the way of life here.

The rainforest echoed with the sounds of both man-made and natural life around him. Winston watched the intricate work Brian was involved in. As the detective, he mused, "So, I hear you've been here a while," while eyeing Brian maneuver a lead pipe he was using to fix a water valve.
"Yep, over a decade now," was Brian's gruff reply, his hands occupied. He paused to wipe his brow with a grimy arm. "It's quite peaceful here, you know."
Winston's gaze lingered on Brian before he divulged, "You were spotted here around the same time Isla was murdered." Their eyes met for a moment before Winston disappeared back into the foliage.

Detective Winston leaned against his cruiser, his eyes tracking the locals as they went about their daily lives. Faces lit up and heads turned as the rhythmic sound of drumming floated through the air. The source of this daily ritual was Jesse, a powerhouse drummer whose status in the town was akin to that of a local hero—a status enjoyed due to his immense talent on the drums.

Winston watched Jesse for a moment longer, taking in the muscles that rippled in his arms as he played. His talent was undeniable, his every beat pounding out a rhythm that seemed to embody the heart of the community itself. He had spent countless hours practicing, strengthening his upper body and arms through his ceaseless devotion to drumming.

Breaking away from the crowd, Winston took the path that led through the rainforest. Evidence suggested that Jesse visited this place often—where he drew inspiration from the symphony of nature itself and penned down melodies. It was known that his best works as a drummer were composed here. Wandering deeper into the rainforest, Winston couldn't help but try to see this place as Jesse might.

A few days ago, Jesse had overheard Isla's nervous whispers about her intent to confess something incriminating to the police, something concerning Jesse himself. The knowledge threw him into a state of unease. Fearing what Isla might reveal about his involvement in illegal activities—activities she had discovered herself—had let the rhythm of Jesse's drumming take a harsher beat.

An association with a metalworking shop came up during the preliminary investigation.  This was the place where Jesse had learned to customize his drumsticks himself, favoring lead piping instead of the usual. It was a small token of uniqueness he added to his music but somehow felt out of sync with the rest.

Returning to his cruiser, Winston pulled out a notepad, flipping to a blank page. Isla's name was written at the top, her connection to Jesse much more than casual. In her possession were the evidence of Jesse's illegal activities capable of damaging, if not entirely ruining Jesse's career and standing in the community.

The pounding of the drums echoed through the stillness of the rainforest, lending an ominous tone to the otherwise peaceful atmosphere. Jesse was aware of his imminent predicament—an inevitable reckoning with his secrets, aided by Isla's confessions.

Another day in the town ended, and with it, Jesse's drumming ceased. But for him, his day was far from over. His routine entailed hours of practice and composing, maintaining his superiority in the art. Jesse's skill was a result of his consistent hard work and dedication, his muscular prowess a testament to both.

For Detective Winston, Jesse was a suspect, committing a crime possibly to protect a secret shrouded by the rhythm of his drums. As he drove away, the murmuring of the locals filled his ears, talking excitedly about Jesse's session for the day. A crime in the community, a rhythm disrupted. The chapter that unfolded was far from melodious.

rounds.evidence_text: In the chilling silence of a hockey rink, Marvin's life was brutally ended with a machete, leaving Detective Winston with two elusive suspects: Justin and Frederick.

Winston sifted through the reports on his desk: the hockey rink homicide, the outlandish murder weapon, the victim known as Marvin who was scheduled to play a hockey game that fateful day. His attention fell onto a single name: Justin.
Leaning back in his chair, Winston found his thoughts weaving around Justin's profession—a piercer; an occupation requiring specific tools like needles and, in Justin's unique case, machetes.

He recalled his past dealings with Justin, particularly how he demonstrated a morose disposition after his proposal got rejected. Winston recalled the desperation in Justin's eyes as he recounted his romantic proposal to Marvin's fiancé. Unfortunately for him, the lady chose Marvin over him.
Justin, who had been frequenting Marvin's hockey games, was there again for the scheduled match. When he arrived, he found Justin waiting amidst the empty seats.

"You watched Marvin's hockey game frequently, yeah?" Winston began, staring up at Justin with a curiosity that was intense. Justin's face distorted with pain as he gave a nod in affirmation, silently communicating his reasons for being there the day of the murder.
Winston shifted on his feet and continued, "You were here that day, weren’t you? To watch Marvin play?"
"I came to watch the game, like always. It was just unfortunate what happened," Justin replied, his voice empty of any emotion.

Winston took a moment before continuing, "I have full CCTV footage of you entering the rink at the time of Marvin's scheduled game, and not leaving until an hour after the murder was supposedly committed."

Pulling out a photo of a distinct, ornate machete from his coat pocket, he asked: "Recognize this? CCTV also shows you carrying a bag into the rink of such size and shape, which could've carried this. And forensics confirmed that this machete, with your piercing studio's distinct engravings, was the murder weapon."
Justin's eyes widened as truthful recognition flashed in them. Winston's next visit would be Justin's piercing parlor.

Justin's piercing studio was like an alternate world. Display cases filled with shiny replicas of machetes were fixed on the walls; a reminder of his unique craft. An odd weapon for a piercer, but it seems it had become Justin's tool of choice. Upon inquiring the staff, he found that only Justin handled these machetes. Furthermore, no other employee had access to them.
His next stop was to Marvin's fiancé, a delicate woman, embodying sorrow and distraught.
"Justin approached you about not marrying Marvin, didn’t he?" Winston struck a direct chord, to which she only nodded, tears welling up in her eyes.

Following the tiring day of investigation, Winston drove back to the precinct. Entering the rink at the time Marvin was scheduled to play, Justin's presence at the murder site, his connection with the weapon, his relations with the victim and Marvin's fiancé - all confirmed by CCTV and forensic evidence, he had gathered ample information. Now, it was time to piece it all together.

The biting chill at the crime scene did nothing to alleviate the morbid spectacle in front of Winston. Marvin's body, brutally murdered with a machete and left on the icy, hockey rink made for an astonishing scene.
Marvin was no saint though. Rumors of his volatile behavior had circulated around town for quite some time.

Having gone through the initial inspection of the crime scene, Winston decided to pay Frederick a visit at his spacious residence next to the cemetery. The presence of Frederick's numerous antique machetes at the crime scene was too much of a coincidence to ignore. The man had far too many in his collection for it to go unnoticed. Frederick, in his role as the curator of the local weapons museum, had unrestricted access to a range of armaments. And curiously, Marvin had been killed with a weapon from Frederick's extensive collection.
Upon reaching the house, Winston noticed Frederick fitting the key into the lock of the cemetery gate, signifying his unrestricted access to the nearby graveyard.

As he walked up to the front porch, he noticed an ominous array of mourning books displayed on a nearby table. He asked about them and Frederick proudly claimed them to be a part of his vast collection documenting rituals from many different cultures.

Upon greeting Frederick, he was immediately shown inside by Frederick's anxious daughter. She was noticeably shaken up from hearing of Marvin's murder, considering that Marvin had recently publicly threatened her.
Upon hearing that, Frederick's reaction was expected. He was an incredibly protective father and the news visibly upset him.
Frederick, seeming desperate to change the topic started talking about his travels, elaborating how he was tasked with visiting and studying the weapons and tombs of ancient cultures.

Sensing Frederick's discomfort, Winston decided to leave the conversation there. He observed his surroundings one final time before thanking them for their hospitality and reminding them to stay safe.
As he strolled back to his car, he noted the machete from Frederick's collection stationed in the museum, something he had been specifically overseeing.

rounds.evidence_text: In the cramped confines of an airplane mid-flight, Zoe was slain using a simple bottle of bleach, propelling Detective Winston into a sky-high murder mystery involving two main suspects: Russell and Alice.

Detective Winston traced his finger along the cleaning supply shelves on the upper deck of Russell's boat, eyeing the bleach conspicuously nestled between a bucket and a scrub brush. The boat bobbed upon the serene waves, while a plane passed overhead, reminding Winston of an earlier sighting.
He remembered seeing Russell boarding that particular plane; a coincidence which became crucial as the case developed.
"Russell," Winston began, involuntarily swaying a bit with the boat's movement, "You use these for cleaning the vessel?"

"Sure do. Learned that during my ship cleanup training. Bleach is requisite for keeping everything in shipshape," the sailor responded, stretching a calloused hand to pick up the vessel. "However, I had a bit of an accident with it once, spilled it on my hands causing harsh chemical burns. Not pleasant, I can tell you."
Russell's face hardened a bit as he set the bleach back in place, adding, somewhat awkwardly, "But what can you do? Matter of training, innit? We all follow procedures."
Winston nodded, making noncommittal noise in agreement. Then, he continued, "Russell, tell me about that trip... the one you took not long ago."
"Oh, that?" Russell scratched his head, "Nothing much to tell, I don't fly often, water is more my domain. But yeah, had to visit family, got a ticket for a coastal ride."
Winston leaned forward, observing Russell's expressions. "By coincidence, Zoe was also on that flight, wasn't she?"
Russell stiffened slightly and Winston noticed the hint of worry crossing his eyes. "Yeah, small world, innit? She was there, sat right beside me for the entirety of the trip."
Inquiring further Winston said, “Did she seem jittery to you, Russell? I Received word that she's been contacting the police for quite some time, reporting offenses she's witnessed.”

Russell responded nervously, "Yeah, heard something similar...It made me uncomfortable, seeing how she started discussing her crime witnessings and all... Well, she even talked about some smuggler group... and I involuntarily disclosed my involvement in questionable activities. Honestly, it felt as if she had seen right through me.”

Winston noticed the worry in Russell's eyes again. He deduced it resulted from Zoe witnessing his wrongdoings and now disclosing these events to others, especially the police. Feeling the tension growing, Winston quickly shifted subjects, “There was even a time when she accepted a drink from you during the flight, didn’t she?”
Russell looked at him, just a hint of surprise in his eyes as he affirmed, "Yes. Yes, she did."

After leaving Russell, Winston couldn't help but think of Zoe and the courage she had exhibited. Zoe had revealed to a close friend about Russell's suspicious actions that looked a lot like drug smuggling. As Winston walked away, he marveled at this young woman's knack for uncovering truths and wondered who’d believe that her penchant for justice would lead her down this turbulent path.

Winston stood at the back of the airplane cabin, dull fluorescent lights casting an artificial pallor over the surrounding faces. There, in an almost eerie calm, sat Alice, the spiritual guru making her way to a retreat with Zoe. Alice was once a flight attendant and used to her guide her companions while flying, as can be seen by the way she carefully selected seats together while booking tickets for herself and Zoe for this flight.

"Alice," Winston began, taking the empty seat next to the spiritual guru. She turned to him, her face flushed and lined with sweat. He noted a fidgety disposition coupled with nervous scratching and almost indecipherable mumbling, but he continued. "I heard you and Zoe were traveling together for a spiritual retreat. And, I remember a gossip at the airport that you specifically saw to it that your seats were together?"
Alice nodded, her hands shaking slightly. "Yes, that's why we bought the tickets together. I always get nervous during flights. Being seated close to my companion helps."
Winston took that in, feeling a certain satisfaction at the beads of sweat dotting Alice's forehead. "And you were helping Zoe adjust with air travel like in your flight attendant days, right?"
"No," Alice said rapidly, her hands touched her chest, and then flittering over the bottles laying around her. "I... I just comfort her with my spiritual methods."

The detective's keen eyes took note of the bottles, their familiarity stinging his brain. Essential oil, but what interested Winston was the similarity they shared in shape and size with another bottle, a bleach bottle he remembered Alice once accidentally swallowed from in her past- the incident which maybe even led her towards understanding the spiritual practices involving bleach ingestion.
"You've got quite the collection of bottles here, Alice."

She nodded hesitatingly, "For my spiritual practices. I was even researching the effects of bleach for cleansing... even after that incident where I accidentally swallowed a sip and had to go to the hospital. It got me interested, you see."

Winston let her words trail off, but his mind was racing. He looked at Zoe's empty seat, her preferred Dragonfruit punch still untouched. The same beverage, Winston noticed, that was in Alice's bag, suspiciously close to the bleach-shaped bottles.
Before Winston got up to leave, he asked casually, "Was it you who had an exchange with an infamous drug dealer some time back? I believe I saw you handing over some money."
Alice's face turned whiter, if possible. "That man... he had a history of selling illegal drugs... but I was only buying... I..."

Winston left her there, mumbling to herself. He had his facts. The mystery wasn't solved, but the clues were there, and Winston turned away as he received a message on his phone. He wondered if the truth went even deeper than it seemed.

rounds.evidence_text: In the sweltering heat of the desert, Detective Winston finds himself amid the ashes of the flamethrower murder of Renee, with Paige and Marianne emerging as the prime suspects.

"May I ask if you were the last person seen with Renee?" Winston asked.
"Yes, detective, I was," Paige answered.

Winston nodded, storing this important information about the dynamics between Paige and Renee. "I have found out from the delivery company that a flamethrower was delivered to this workshop recently. Was it yours? The one you ordered?"

"Yes, that's correct," Paige replied, her face unchanging. "You see, I work in special effects. I deal with all sorts of contraptions, including flamethrowers. They're not as deadly as they seem, you know? Only in the wrong hands..."

It seemed like Paige was positioning herself just within the edge of suspicion, but Winston kept his thoughts to himself, a stoic expression fixed on his face. He then asked about Paige's closeness with the desert, a quick detour from her workshop.

"Oh, it's easily accessible. I often take a walk to clear my head," she replied, "And Renee knew about my frequent trips there, that's why it wasn't unusual for her when I told her I wanted to show her something in the desert."

"Marianne." He called to the barista working behind the counter.
"Yes sir, what can I get you?" She looked up with a plastered service smile that Winston had seen more often than he'd like to admit.
"Coffee, black," he added.

Marianne was usually a woman of few words. It was already known in the café that Marianne, although a people person during work hours, preferred solitude outside of work. She was somewhat enigmatic, leaving work as soon as her shift ended without any explanation about her after-work plans. It was a habit she diligently stuck to, against curious coworkers who often loiter around longer.
"Winston, aren't you?" She handed over the coffee, her facial expression gave away nothing. She had a breed of indifference that he found puzzling.
"Yeah, you remember." He toasted his coffee cup, looking at the foam art on its surface.

Curiously, after one of her visits, a flamethrower was found missing from the shop - the owner had confirmed it himself, ruffling through the shop inventory in disbelief. A particular stock draw from the shop should technically be tagged a coincidence and yet, here he was.
"So, how'd you end up here?" Winston decided to put out some line, in search of a bite.
"Needed a job, this did me good," she stated curtly, keeping it decidedly professional.
"I hear you gotta get fire safety certification to keep the espresso machines running and avoid mishaps. That true?" He ventured further.
"Yeah, mandatory stuff." She added, the impenetrable exterior still intact.
"That's neat, handy skills I reckon." He sipped his coffee, testing the waters.

That's when he remembered the rumors – Marianne had been arrested for a theft charge. Worse yet, she was found guilty and now, a court date next week awaiting sentencing. It all seemed to tie back to an unfortunate event in the desert involving an individual named Renee, who had testified against Marianne in court. Not just a common run-in-the-mill victim, but linked to Marianne with a web of unknown connections.
"What time do you get off work?" He asked, catching her off guard.
"I...like to go straight home." She fumbled her words. The confession about her arrest seemed to take the wind out of her sails.

After a small chat about the dry weather, Winston mentioned he was headed to the pawn shop down the road, on the trail of the missing flamethrower, leaving a hint of a departing farewell. She turned to the wall clock as soon as the shop door jingled shut - the end of her shift almost due. Winston absorbed this behavior, letting his gaze linger for one more moment before setting off.

"And the time... when exactly did it happen?" Justin changed the topic right back to the crime again, the flame in his eyes burning brighter at the prospect of new details.
Winston frowned slightly, "During the game," he answered, watching Justin's face carefully. He appeared unphased.
Justin cocked a brow, excitement mixed with intrigue evident in his lit eyes. "I was here during that time," he pointed out, "Watching the game."

Winston nodded, "You were, and as far as anyone knows, you didn't leave until well after," he almost sighed, "Listen Justin, what exactly is it with you and this crime? It seems that you're more interested in it than the hockey game."

Justin shifted, looking anywhere but at him, "Well, it's just...Marvin and his fiancé, you know. I just thought they...weren't right for each other. I had a talk with her once. I asked her not to marry him. But she didn't listen."

The harsh, industrial lighting of the hockey rink painted a grave picture as Detective Winston surveyed the crime scene. Setting that evidence aside, Winston trotted towards the museum, a place Frederick frequented due to his love for antique machetes. Frederick had the responsibility of overseeing the unique collection of blades, his dedication emanating as bright as the lights above the collection.

What piqued Winston's interest though was that one of the machetes in Frederick's collection matched the description of the weapon that ended Marvin's life. "Marvin once threatened Frederick's girl. Frederick didn't take it lightly, and they've been arguing ever since," the coworker confessed. Despite the locker rooms being an area exclusively accessed by staff with keys, Marvin had been spotted in there more times than anyone could count.
Winston's sharp gasp caught the coworkers attention, "What is it, Detective?"
"Nothing...just...let me know if you notice anything else...odd," replied Winston.
Echoes off the old lockers were the only responses he got.

rounds.evidence_text: In the dense, dank heart of the rainforest, Skylar's life was brutally silenced with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a labyrinth of lies, offered up by the two prime suspects - Albert and Mya.

His gaze shifted to a tall woman energetically engaging with her relatives, her vibrant energy palpable amongst the crowd. That would be Mya, the adventurous cousin of the unfortunate victim, Skylar.
He noticed the polished locket adorning her neck, catching the light beautifully, but a sombre contrast to its owner's lively charm.
Exuding friendly charm, Winston approached her, "Mya, may I have a couple of moments?"
"Of course, detective. How may I help you?"
"I understand you and Skylar used to explore your adventurous side together," Winston mentioned casually, trying not to stir any emotional discomfort.
Mya's face softened, "Yes. We both shared a love for the wilderness. Just last week, she invited me on a camping trip to the rainforest. It was harmonious escapades until…” she trailed off.

“Aye, I’m sorry for your loss, Mya.”  
 
Winston noticed the emphasis on her well-toned physique - a strong and agile body, built on a rigorous exercise routine and several hiking and mountain climbing expeditions successfully completed over the years.

Later on, Winston got an opportunity to evaluate the surveillance video of the day Skylar went missing. A quiet scene it was, with only a single instance of incoming and no outgoing traffic - a four-wheel-drive carrying two adventurous souls - Skylar and Mya - into the depths of the rainforest.

Winston’s keen eyes caught the glimpse of Mya’s camping gear. It sure was well stocked - ropes, food supplies, a lead pipe, tents, boots… A lead pipe. The very same, that had turned brutal enough to end a life in the tranquil rainforest.
At Mya’s, while she was away, Winston could only find her camping gear partially scattered in disarray. The lead pipe was blatantly missing.

In a cruiser parked down the street, Winston watched Mya jog up to the deadly rainforest, maybe a run to process her grief, or maybe it was part of her regular exercise routine. Winston watched Mya stoop suddenly and pick something up. A glint of gold. Later, at the reunion, the piece was identified as Skylar’s locket around Mya’s neck. A locket that mysteriously went missing after Skylar's demise and never returned to the rightful inheritors.
Winston took a deep breath. There was so much more to untangle in the mysterious disappearance of Skylar. The case continued to thicken, deeper into the rainforest.

Casual drizzle splattered against the umbrella of Winston as he stood by the yellow cab, its windows slick with rain and partially hiding the figure inside. He knocked twice against the window before it hesitantly slid down, revealing the rough and worn face of Albert, a cab driver who had been working these city streets for longer than most would care to remember.
"Albert," Winston began, pulling out his badge to cut off any question of his identity. "Seems like you're having a quiet night."
"Just like every other night in this forsaken city," Albert responded bitterly, his hands, the hands of a man used to hard labor, tightening around the taxi steering wheel.

"I heard about your baseball career back in college. Must have been exciting times," Winston remarked, casually glancing at a lead pipe secured beneath the driver's seat. "Got to make sure feelings of nostalgia don't lead to some baseball practice, especially not in a city like ours."
Albert hesitated for a moment, before answering, "It's for safety. Different times…"

Winston nodded, turning towards the rainforest in the distance. Albert followed his gaze, "Crazy what happened. I was just driving her, Skylar...that is, to the rainforest. The city loved her, I've even seen people switch cabs to ride with her."
"Must have been a challenge," Winston said, subtly hinting at the power dynamics at play.
"It was more than just a challenge," Albert growled. "That woman was taking away everything I had."
"Do you know why she wanted to go to the rainforest?" Winston asked, eager to shift the focus.

"Didn't ask," Albert responded briskly. "She requested me as her driver and asked to go to the rainforest. Took a little detour, tried to show her some city charm...wouldn't say she really appreciated it though."
"Do you know if anyone else was with her there?"
"Just her," Albert answered. "As far as I knew, it was just going to be her in the rainforest. That was the last I saw."

As Winston walked away, leaving Albert with his rumbling taxi and burdensome thoughts, he pondered how volatile resentment could become if not managed properly — a flame which could engulf the careers and lives of even those most loved. The rain pattered against his umbrella, but beneath it, his mind was turning.

rounds.evidence_text: In the deafening silence of an unexpectedly deserted fitness center, Detective Winston finds himself staring at a chilling scene - Isaac's lifeless body riddled with shotgun pellets, leaving Milton and Alice as his primary suspects.

The old dusty building sat in the middle of downtown, open 24 hours to cater to the city-life fitness enthusiasts. The 24-hour timing of the gym provided Isaac a place to be when he was working late. It also afforded Milton, the alleged tax evader and the building owner, numerous opportunities to encounter Isaac.

For years Winston had known about the gym, a small struggling space owned and operated by Isaac, an IRS agent turned yoga instructor, who had been found dead there the previous night - shot dead with what appeared to be a shotgun. Isaac, with his whistleblowing nature, had recently acquired extensive evidence on a tax evasion scheme. This scheme was alleged to be run by none other than Milton.

Milton adjusted the strap of his shotgun before answering, "He was a tenant. That's all."
Winston furrowed his brows, "That shotgun - it's legal!"
"Indeed," Milton declared, "I even passed the required training course. The local authorities granted me a license."
Winston's eyes darted to the keys in the man's hand, "I see you also have keys to the gym."
"It's my property, Detective," Milton responded dismissively.
Winston sighed, unfazed by Milton's audacity, "It's undisputed that the gym is never locked yet Isaac was alone last night. He had potential evidence that could have sent you to prison, Milton."
"So?" Milton's face revealed no fear and no hint of adversity.

This reaction gnawed at Winston as he returned to his car. Thoughts of Isaac's murder - the shotgun wound matching the one Milton regularly carried, Milton's unfazed demeanor despite the possible charges, and Milton's evident firearms training - swarmed his mind. As he mulled over these facts, he made a mental note to delve deeper into Isaac's evidence - the potential key to exposing Milton's illicit activities and ensuring justice.

Winston squinted his eyes, scanning the familiar hustle and bustle of the fitness center. The crime scene of Isaac's murder was abnormal, the contrast of violence against the backdrop of health and vitality.

Dodging a stray basketball, he made his way to the bench where Alice and Isaac used to workout together regularly. Alice had a spotless record with the fitness center - seemed she had never missed a month of membership dues.

"Hello Alice," he initiated the conversation. He knew patience was key in such delicate interrogations, especially with suspects like Alice.
"Oh, Winston, what an unexpected surprise!" Alice's face lit up with genuine surprise, her eyes shifting to the shotgun propped at the corner of the bench, its presence undeniable.
Discarding any pleasantries, Winston moved to the crux of the matter. "Isaac trained right here didn’t he, you guys used to train together?"
Alice gave a small nod, memories flickering in her eyes. Winston observed her, recognizing a trace of melancholy. Alice’s dulcet voice broke the silence. "Yes...we had a sort of routine together."

He glanced at her bruised knuckles appreciatively, a new patch of purple catching his attention. Her friends had mentioned Alice's weekly fight club rendezvous every Tuesday night. The tough soldier, habituated to the brutality of the fight club, would invariably return home every Wednesday morning nursing fresh battle sores.

Alice was a puzzle piece in a complex jigsaw puzzle. An aunt, a loyal fitness center member, a fighter, and undoubtedly an experienced shotgun user due to her military background. Her every Tuesday night fights stood out starkly against her normal routine. She was a conundrum tightly bound by her routine, fitness center membership, military background, and her recent shotgun purchase.

"You know Winston...Isaac was the only family I had left," Alice mused, her thoughts clearly going down a memory lane, her fingers tracing her recent shotgun casually. The shotgun she had recently purchased was now in her possession. With these words, she abruptly stood up, signaled the trainer for her next routine, leaving Winston to join the dots of the puzzle she represented in this murder mystery.

rounds.evidence_text: In the lush yet perilous heart of the rainforest, Frances' life was brutally ended by a shotgun blast, and now, within the deceptive calm, Detective Winston is probing Meredith and Kinsley under the weight of suspicion.

Buster, her faithful Golden Retriever was whining nearby, his normally luminous fur matted and dirty. Winston made a note to have someone pick up the poor dog, and that's when he remembered Jerry, the local birdwatcher, mentioning that he'd seen Meredith near this spot around the time the murder would have occurred.

Meredith... the pet groomer who'd often take walks in these woods for her job. She worked nearby, grooming the pets of the affluent folks who didn't mind living a little closer to nature. Hopefully, she could shed some light on things.

"Hey there, detective! How can I help you today?"

Winston stood near the cordon tape at the crime scene. Frances, a law enforcement officer, had been working relentlessly to bring down the local gang. According to her case files, Frances' investigations have been troublesome for many, especially those involved in dirty deals with the gang. Ever since she started investigating the intersections between Kinsley's spiritual group and the gang, she had drawn close to exposing the hidden ties and nefarious deals between them.
“In all my years in the force,” Winston said to his partner, "I've seen some hard characters, but spiritual gurus and gang members tied together?"
His partner shrugged, "What's the world coming to, huh?"

Days later, Winston met Kinsley, a spiritual guru who had been seen leading his spiritual group in the forest the day Frances was killed. Frances, who had been present in the forest on that day, shared her doubts about Kinsley's practices and friends, including those in the gang. She had even observed the pair of them sequestered away in a corner of the forest, a scene that appeared strange given the circumstances.
Winston leveled a steady gaze at Kinsley, "So you were here in the forest with Frances on the day she was murdered?"
Kinsley nodded, a serene smile never leaving his face, "I was guiding my disciples here on the same day."
He went on to add, "In fact, Frances did join me at one point. With just the two of us, we engaged in a brief yet hearty conversation about life, spirituality, and the power of transformation."
"But you don't use any digital communication platforms for your group, correct?" Winston asked. It had given him a headache trying to get in contact with Kinsley or gather more information about him.

Kinsley merely smiled, "We believe in living in the moment, Detective. Our connection is a spiritual one, untouched by the likes of Facebook, Twitter, or Instagram."
"As such, you only announce your public events on your website, with no social media pages connected to it?" Winston pressed.
"That's the way I prefer it," Kinsley was nonchalant, "Avoids a lot of unnecessary distractions, wouldn't you agree?"

Looking around the peaceful setting, Winston had to reassess his definition of 'distraction'. What wasn't peaceful though, was Kinsley's openly acknowledged links between his spiritual group and the local gang, which added a disturbing edge to his spiritual pursuits.
Winston found it necessary to probe, "I do find it peculiar that a spiritual guru like you would publicly acknowledge your group's ties with the local gang. That's... quite interesting."
Kinsley simply shrugged, "I have always believed in the power of transformation, Detective. Everyone deserves a chance, don't they?"

With that final statement, Kinsley rose from his seat, effectively ending their conversation. The case was beginning to appear murkier than before. Winston knew there were still critical pieces of this puzzle he needed to uncover.

rounds.evidence_text: In the unsettling calm of the zoo, the peculiar death of Walter by a nail gun sets Detective Winston on a challenging trail of clues, with Glenn and Dennis as prime suspects.

Winston exhaled a stream of smoke as he looked over his notes once more. There were five previous sightings of a man at the local zoo, groceries in hand, and each and every one of them connected to one individual - Glenn. He also found a receipt from the grocery store where Glenn works, it was a purchase for nails specifically for a nail gun.
Remembering a recent eyewitness report of a man on the day of the murder, Winston recalled the description of a man being similar to Glenn, who was spotted carrying a bulky tool bag.

"Glenn?" Winston called out, getting the clerk's attention. Glenn turned, his round face projecting innocence.
"Can I help you?" He replied, offering Winston a smile.
"Winston Phillips, homicide," he introduced himself, flashing his badge briefly.
"Has there, uh, been a murder or something?" Glenn asked, feigning obliviousness.
"You could say that," Winston confirmed, "Could I ask where you were yesterday, Glenn?"
Glenn paused, scratching the back of his head before answering, "Took my little girl to the zoo. We've got a membership there. We always watch the monkeys get fed, it's always at the same time."
Winston's eyebrow lifted slightly. This matches the eyewitness reports placing Glenn at the zoo that day, and another reporting a bulky blue bag on his person.
"A tool bag to the zoo, Glenn?" Winston raised the question.
Glenn’s smile started to fade, "I usually carry it around with me for work, it's got all my tools." He said, a flicker of unease in his eyes, "In case I need them, you know."

Winston found these elements forming a clear image, but he knew better than to impress suspicion where it wasn't explicitly warranted. He would need more. More conversations, more observations, and more unearthing of Glenn’s peculiar behaviours.

Detective Winston brushed crumbs of his sandwich onto his pile of case files. His latest, involving a man named Walter, was proving rather intriguing. Winston squinted his eyes at the witness statement in front of him, given by the key character in this tragedy, a man named Dennis.
