rounds.evidence_text: In the cramped confines of an airplane mid-flight, Zoe was slain using a simple bottle of bleach, propelling Detective Winston into a sky-high murder mystery involving two main suspects: Russell and Alice.

As detective Winston stared at the boarded up airplane on the tarmac, his mind churned over the limited evidence he had at his disposal. Zoe, the cheerful flight stewardess was the victim, and he was about to interview one of the contentious suspects - a sailor by trade, a man named Russell. Detective Winston had seen him earlier that day. He was watching from a distance as Russell, with animal carcasses in tow, disappeared into his home. Winston didn't believe he had ever come across a more unique assortment of characters in any of his previous investigations. He sighed and decided it was time to meet with Russell, his main course of inquiry for the day.

Making his way to the docking area in the early morning light, he spotted a weathered sailor hunching over a bucket filled with cleaning supplies on his trawler. Bleach was prominent among them, a bottle of it sitting half used on the washed deck. As Winston approached, Russell began to explain how he had unintentionally injured himself in the past while cleaning his boat with the very same bleach. Despite the painful memory, it seemed he was determined to keep his ship sparking and sanitary as per his sailor training.

During their conversation, Russell mentioned his aesthetics and love for taxidermy, a skill he had picked up during one of his various trips abroad, in particular, a trip to Norway. He explained how he always tried to learn something new from every country he visited, and Norway taught him taxidermy. "And then there's my taxidermy workshop at home, in the basement," Russell revealed, "...probably filled with dust bunnies now." He even told Winston about several animal carcasses he planned to work with later that evening in his basement workshop.

Feeling he had gained his trust, Winston eased into the events which transpired in the airplane, "You boarded the flight with Zoe, correct?" Russell nodded, wrinkling his already weather-worn face. He began to retell his version of events. Winston noted that Russell started with how he found himself sitting next to Zoe on the airplane, further deepening their connection. From shared cab glasses to a friendly conversation which culminated in Russell offering Zoe a drink during the flight, the events were building up to an intricate narrative. Winston stored away these significant details which included their seating arrangement on the flight, to review later.

As the day wore on, Winston decided to wrap up his inquiry. Confirming with Russell his ticket receipt and presence on the same flight with Zoe, he felt he was making progress. An observing officer had provided his statement of seeing Russell board the same plane as Zoe. This was slowly shaping up into a complex murder mystery involving a sailor, bleach, taxidermy, and air travel. Winston ended his day at a local bar, quietly replaying the events of the day, piecing together this unique puzzle to get closer to the truth.

The piercing glare of Detective Winston enveloped the flamboyant spiritual guru Alice, as she walked towards him under the high terminal ceilings of the airport. Clad in flowing robes with bottles of various shapes and sizes dangling from her belt, she confidently greeted him.
"Detective Winston, I was expecting you. After all, one doesn't have to be a spiritual guru to know that after what happened, the police would want answers."
Winston viewed her flamboyant getup briefly and caught sight of the wide variety of bottles she lugged around. Among them were the weirdly familiar-looking bleach bottles.

Alice's past as a flight attendant was no secret. Through that career, she also formed a close bond with Zoe. They recently boarded a plane together in order to attend a spiritual retreat. Alice had been meticulous in arranging the journey, purchasing tickets specifically for seats next to each other.

Sundrenched in conversation, one fact kept flashing in Winston's mind. Zoe had found documents against Alice; a heap of paperwork that cast these spiritual practices in a harsh and fraudulent light. One crucial point Alice admitted to was being present when Zoe discovered these damning papers.

A gentle rustling of papers revealed that Alice had also seen Zoe making copies of these records. In the ambiguous silence, Alice poured herself a drink from one of her many bottles. She couldn't help but mention Zoe's preference for the same beverage that she carried in the same bag where the bleach-like bottles sat nestled.
"I accidentally sipped bleach once," Alice suddenly offered up, piling pressure on the unsaid words looming between them. "The hospital visit wasn't pleasant."
The detective's eyes shifted from Alice to her hands. The bottles she was carrying flaunts similar size and shape to that of a bleach bottle.
"There is this spiritual cleansing practice," Alice continued, "It involves the ingestion of bleach. Out of curiosity, I researched its effects. Nothing serious, just trying to learn more about it."
Winston nodded, carefully treading around the probing questions he wanted to ask, knowing this was not the time to draw any conclusions.

rounds.evidence_text: In the eerie silence of a moonlit swamp, Leroy's life was gruesomely ended by a sai, setting the stage for Detective Winston's most perplexing murder investigation yet, with suspects Clayton and Madelyn cloaked in mystery.

Under the glaring afternoon sun, Detective Winston stood at the edge of the swamp, the muck and murkiness of the water reflecting back the solemnity in his eyes. Murder always had a way of turning the beauty of the world eerie, each flutter of nature appearing as if it was whispering the secrets of the dark act committed here.
Leroy, it seemed, had met his end here, impaled by a sai. It was a martial arts weapon distinct in its deadly simplicity, known all too well by the martial arts community.
Winston mulled over the circumstances surrounding Leroy's death. Leroy had gotten married to Clayton's ex-wife shortly after they had filed for divorce.

Leaving the scene, Winston drove the short distance to the local dojo owned and run by a man by the name of Clayton. Clayton was an ex-husband to the recent bride of Leroy, and an avid martial arts instructor. According to whispers among the locals, he seemed to be a man still inherently in love with his ex-wife, a flame that lulled even after their love had supposedly extinguished.

On driving to the dojo, nostalgic flashes of visits to the local bar sprung forth in Winston's mind. Memories of how locals had on multiple occasions, narrated tales of Clayton exploring the swamp alone and of how he also ran survival tours there. On the day of the murder, many people at the local bar saw Clayton getting into his car alone, painting a picture of his solitary routine.
Upon arriving, he found Clayton, kneeling before an illustrious collection of martial arts weaponry, that included a sai, the same weapon used in the murder of Leroy.
"So, you collect these?" Winston asked, nodding at the weapons.
"It's part of the job," Clayton responded as he carefully set down the sai, "having a wide knowledge of martial arts weaponry. But yes, I have developed a personal collection."
Winston ventured further, "I heard you run survival tours in the swamp."
Clayton chuckled. "Oh yes. I love exploring the swamp. It's like it's a part of me. Each corner, each nook, I know all of them like the back of my hand.”
Winston then mentioned Clayton's recent loss. "Your ex got married to Leroy shortly after your divorce... Must've been a real punch in the gut," he said, gauging Clayton’s reaction.

Clayton grimaced then muttered, "Well, yeah, of course. Can't deny it stung a bit."  
"But you'd want her back--"
Without waiting for Winston to finish, Clayton interjected. "Yes, I would. But she made it clear she doesn't want a reconciliation as long as Leroy is around."

As Winston left the dojo, he began to storyboard the potential narrative. A man still in love with his ex-wife who wed another man right after their divorce, seen alone on the day of her new husband’s murder, with a confession that the ex-wife did not want to reconcile as long as Leroy was alive. He had a lot to ponder.

Detective Winston strode into the lobby of the martial arts gym, taking in the sights of many people practicing their moves, some more graceful than others. His attention quickly moved to a woman near the back of the room, demonstrating a jarring, yet elegant, technique to her student with a sai. Recognizing her from a picture at his precinct, Winston confirmed it was Madelyn.

He recalled Leroy’s fitness schedule, and his plans to switch personal trainers, leaving Madelyn for her biggest competitor. Friends had mentioned conversations Leroy had with Madelyn's rival. Winston also knew from his sources, she had been in the vicinity when Leroy was on the phone discussing the change.

Madelyn had a reputation of changing her hair practically every week. She seemed to enjoy the variety and surprise. A confirmed fact when Winston had visited her residential premises discovering several multi-colored wigs.

Not wasting any time, Winston approached Madelyn after her demonstration. Madelyn agreed to go to the local coffee shop for a friendly chat. After a sputtered start, Winston was able to get Madelyn talking about her martial arts training, including the sai technique she used in her demonstration. A technique he knew was the cause of Leroy’s death.

Her unique weapon choice hadn't really surprised him. Given the dimension of martial arts Madelyn specialized in, he suspected the sai came from her collection. A trip to the local martial arts store had led him to a store owner who confirmed her recent purchase of a pair. As well, the owner remembered seeing Madelyn practicing with her new acquisition at a local gym.

Eventually, Winston brought up the subject of passports. He'd found an interesting assortment of passports in various names inside a filing cabinet at Madelyn's house. He recalled her flustered behavior earlier at the post office where she'd been spotted getting passport photos taken. She struggled to explain, her face blanching at what he might uncover.

The conversation ended on a note of betrayal, with Madelyn softly admitting her inner circle betrayals. Winston gathered the facts in his mind, of hair wigs, martial arts and betrayal. Whisking the rest of his untouched coffee, he left Madelyn at the table, lost in her own world of memories.

Yet Winston had a murder inquiry to solve and no amount of color-changing wigs or phony passports could disguise that fact. He walked away with a nod, thinking of the next steps he would take before approaching Madelyn again. Irrespective of what she chose to conceal, he believed in the truth unveiling itself, the truth of a victim named Leroy.

rounds.evidence_text: In the heart of a brawling wrestling ring, Cecil lay lifeless, a bullet his final opponent, marking the onset of a complex investigation for Detective Winston with suspects Tiffany and Theresa under the spotlight.

Winston lit a cigarette and took a moment to stare at the wrestling ring. The ropes held weighty silence, which is the exact opposite of what they were intended for. A far cry from the usual cheers and energy which should have filled the stadium that night as Cecil was scheduled to wrestle.

Exiting the stadium, Winston eased himself into his car and navigated the streets toward the home of Theresa, the victim's ex-girlfriend. As he made his way, he noticed a billboard with Cecil's face on it, advertising a recent public event where Cecil had appeared with a different woman, acknowledging their new relationship for the first time.

He stopped at a red light and tried to shake off an image of Theresa and Cecil together. Scrolling through social media on her phone, Theresa gasping with surprise, throwing the phone across the room, suffering, alone...

"Focus, Winston," he whispered to himself as he stopped in front of a house. As he rang the doorbell, he couldn't help but remember a detail he had come across while going through the night of the murder. Theresa was seen entering the wrestling ring that night, and to talk to Cecil, or so she claimed.
"Detective, you here for Theresa?" a middle-aged woman opened the door and asked, pulling him out of his thoughts.
"Actually, I'm here to talk with her about Cecil," Winston handed the woman his card.

"I suppose you'll want to know about this." She motioned for him to follow her up the stairs to Theresa's room. The woman, who happened to be Theresa's mother, and a police officer, pointed towards a certificate.
"That is from a gun safety course she attended last year," she said. "A course I insisted my little girl to take once she borrowed my off-duty pistol."
Strange, Winston thought, as Theresa's mom changed the topic. She mentioned that Theresa had tried to get back together with Cecil time and again, but only to face rejection each time.
"She was emotionally charged that night and failed to hide it," her mother sighed. "Being around Cecil wasn't easy for my girl, you understand, right?"

Winston gave a curt nod, mind gathering threads, weaving possibilities, but never concluding. He concluded his conversation, thanked Theresa's mother for her time, and walked out to his car. It was just another puzzle piece in this mysterious jigsaw he was tarrying to make sense of - A flower girl, a wrestling match, and an unexpected turn of love.

Winston rubbed his temples, a familiar migraine beginning to make its presence known. He gathered the crime scene photos; among the images was a picture of a pistol found hidden within the bar. Authorities had confirmed it as the murder weapon for Cecil's death. He gave them another look and with a resigned sigh, shoved them into a drawer. Cecil's death had stirred up the city like nothing he had ever seen. Killed right in the middle of a wrestling match. Well, not quite in the middle. The match had ended late at Tiffany's bar where Cecil had been a referee.

He sank into the battered chair in front of Tiffany, taking in her imposing figure. Tiffany, a woman who was frequently seen by patrons at the bar, not only when she was working her bartending shifts but also sharing drinks with her boyfriend too. She was a fixture here, familiar to all patrons. The wrestling match had occurred at her bar that night, and according to the countless depositions, she was often seen at the bar, tidying up even during wrestling matches.
"So you were at the bar when the wrestling match ended?" Winston asked, breaking the silence.
"Yes." She replied curtly. "I work every night."
"Even on the nights of the wrestling matches?" Winston inquired casually.
"Yes, even then. Business is business." Tiffany responded, avoiding eye contact.
Winston took out his notepad and began to scribble something. "What do you do here after the bar closes?"
Tiffany shifted in her seat, "Well, after the wrestling match, I clean up, I am typically the last person here since I am the only one who takes care of the cleaning."
"Did you see anyone else around when you were leaving?" Winston asked purposely vague.
Tiffany hesitated, "Well...a regular customer saw me meet with someone after closing. Shifty, he called him. He wasn't anyone I thought to worry about, just an old friend."
"So you didn’t know that according to the same regular customer who saw you outside, this 'Shifty' character had multiple outstanding warrants for his arrest?” Winston pressed.
Tiffany blazed red but didn't respond. Opting to change the subject, Winston asked about her conceal carry permit.

"Yes, I applied for a permit a while back." She admitted, glancing warily at the photos Winston laid out on the table, a picture of the pistol found concealed within the bar's refuse as though tossed away in a hurry.
"Any reason as to why?" Winston asked nonchalantly.
"There's a lot of undesirable elements floating around here detective, a girl's got to feel safe," she said, avoiding his gaze.

Winston nodded, scribbling down another note. He leaned back in his chair, gaze focused on Tiffany, "Patrons have frequently shared stories of overheard gang-related conversations between you and your boyfriend whenever you're here. Care to explain that?"
Tiffany stiffened, "We talk about a lot of things detective, that doesn't mean we're doing anything illegal."

"I see." Winston concluded, rising from his chair. Winston knew he had to return to the precinct. There were still interviews to conduct and leads to chase. The facts were piling up and creating an unsettling picture. But it was up to the jury now to decide who was the murderer and who was merely in the wrong place at the wrong time.

rounds.evidence_text: In the bustling labyrinth of a city mall, a grisly murder sends shockwaves as Xenia is killed with a nail gun, leaving Detective Winston with two perplexing suspects: Van and Wilfred.

Detective Winston felt his chest tighten slightly as he stepped onto the crime scene. Another murder, and this time - a shopping mall. Xenia, the victim, a blond woman in her early forties. Falling under the jurisdiction of his detective expertise, Winston gathered the scattered bits of facts and evidence that were available up to this point.

The murder weapon, a nail gun, an unusual choice. That fact alone put Winston’s investigation into a small percentage of the population who had access to such tools - contractors. And with this unfortunate coincidence was the fact that the nail gun used in the crime was reported missing from Wilfred's construction project, which made for even a more compelling lead to pursue.

Court sessions were known to be highly stressful, creating a complete sense of tension in the courtroom, causing lawyers like Wilfred to sweat profusely. Yet, even under such stressful circumstances Wilfred always maintained a fresh scent.
Upon hearing this, his mind immediately turned to Wilfred, a local lawyer who was a known aficionado of construction, something that would give him easy access to nail guns.
Winston sent out a request for surveillance footage of Wilfred's construction site, hoping to gain some insight into whether Wilfred had any interaction with nail guns.

He also requested the mall’s CCTV footage, given that Xenia was killed in the mall. The footage verified Wilfred’s presence in the mall around the same time Xenia was murdered. But that wasn't the evidence that caught Winston’s eye. It was the traces of bakery flour, always noticeable on Wilfred's shoes.

Wilfred was known to spend significant amounts of time on his feet in the courtroom, often sweating profusely due to the stressful court sessions. Yet a remarkable trait about Wilfred was that he maintained a fresh scent, even after a long day. This always intrigued Winston; however, upon further investigation, he discovered Wilfred's secret was the luxury of having a bathroom with a shower in his office; thus the puzzle started to come together.

The authorities were unsure of Wilfred's exact location during the murder. Nobody could verify his whereabouts and the time Xenia was killed, Wilfred was unaccounted for, posing a substantial mystery for Winston to solve.

As he continued his investigation, Winston implemented a strategic approach to obtain more information. He planned a meeting with Wilfred under the pretext of discussing a case, and at the scheduled meeting, he carefully observed the unassuming lawyer.
"When's the last time you visited your construction project, Wilfred?" Winston asked, keeping a close eye on the man's reactions.
"Monday, as I recall," Wilfred responded, not missing a beat. "Why do you ask?"
"Just curiosity. You ever handle a nail gun before?"
Wilfred offered a nonchalant shrug. "Sure. Comes with the territory."
Winston noted the answer, pressing further. "And how about the mall? Been there recently?”
Wilfred nodded, stating, "Oh, yes, a couple of times this week."

In the end, Winston came out of the meeting with more questions than answers, but the strings of information were beginning to shape a premise. One thing was certain - Wilfred was irrefutably intertwined in this case.
Winston swept through the shopping mall like water, eyes scanning, earpiece transmitting information straight to the station. He was looking for Van, who had been on shift when Xenia was killed.
He spotted a muscular man with a nametag was unloading boxes from a service entrance, huffing and puffing as he went. "Looks like our guy," he mumbled into his headset.
"I've been expecting you," said Van, the bodybuilder, wiping his sweat-drenched forehead with a well-charred sleeve. He pointed to a chair across the table, "Have a seat, will you?"
Winston did, and before he even opened his mouth, Van was speaking, "You know, Xenia was here almost every day. She loved this place, loved shopping. Sad thing what happened."
Winston, not one for small talk, started grilling Van, "You were on shift when she was killed, right Van?"
"Yeah, I was," he replied. "I ain't seen nothing though."
"What does your job entail?"  Winston asked, changing the subject.
"I've got free run of this place. Lock, stock and barrel, I can move about as I please,” Van said, directing an intense look at Winston's face.

Bryan hesitated for a moment, weighing his words. "About all of his mockery... it's been tough," Bryan said, avoiding Winston's gaze.  "He's been parading around, telling everyone that I've been stealing. He even found a way to publicize I've been dipping into our petty cash."
Winston nodded, trying not to show his surprise. Travis, that jolly, carefree soul resorting to humiliation and accusations? Hard to believe.
"Seems like you've been quite worried about jail, huh, Bryan? Aren't you scared of these accusations?"

"Y-yes... I... I can't go to jail, detective. That’s my worst nightmare, I ..." Bryan faltered, his hand instinctively brushing over his jeans where Winston could spot the handle of his sharpened hatchet, just peeking out, its shine all too prominent.

Winston settled in at his desk, running his fingers over the cold, metallic edges of the woodworking tools that lay strewn across his workspace. They were in evidence bags, cataloged meticulously. A particular hatchet caught his eye, one that lab results had confirmed as the murder weapon. It belonged to Everett, who managed his own private collection of woodworking tools.

Everett, a curator with a keen interest in woodworking, worked at a museum dedicated to the craft. His tools, his museum job, the woodworking... along with these, evidence bags with Everett's paragliding equipment caught Winston's eye. They were marked as found at the murder site, logged and stored.
Deviating from his thoughts about woodworking, Winston began browsing through the case profiles scrolling across his screen.

Travis, the victim, was a paragliding aficionado who had recently earned an international award within the sport—a revered distinction that Everett had also vied for failing to clinch. It seemed Everett struggled for the same acclaim, without much luck.

Everett's paragliding equipment, now part of the collected evidence from the murder site, was a strong indictor. This was where Travis had met his end. Coincidently the same place where a paragliding event was held that day.
Straightening up and pocketing his notebook, Winston decided to pay a visit to Everett at the museum.
Whilst there, he noticed Everett skilfully fashioning a piece of wood into a bird’s wing. Maybe it was the context, but it struck him the resemblance it bore to a paraglider's wing.
“Detective Winston,” Everett greeted him, offering a firm, rugged handshake. “Care for a tour?”
Winston declined the offer. “I hear you and Travis were at the same paragliding meetup that day,” Winston started with a nonchalant shrug of his shoulders.
Everett, with a somber nod, confirmed his attendance at said meetup. He muttered something about always being in Travis’ shadow, causing Winston to raise his brow in intrigue.

Before leaving the museum, he waved down a few visitors, asking if they also shared an interest in paragliding. To his surprise, all of them recalled seeing Everett’s vehicle parked at the site of the meetup that day, matching the timings of the murder deeds.

With the image of the hatchet from Everett's collection - the very one identified as the murder weapon - Everett's paragliding gear found at the crime scene, and the chilling timeline coming together, Winston stepped back into the early evening humidity, a new sense of the suspect's world giving weight to his thoughts. But, those dots could wait for another day to connect. For now, it was time to head back to the precinct.

rounds.evidence_text: In the hallowed silence of a synagogue, a shocking murder unfolds as Derek is impaled by a harpoon, leaving Detective Winston with two unlikely suspects – Hailey and Angela.

Winston idly flicked his cigarette ash onto the pavement as he studied the crime scene photos spread out on the hood of his car. His stone-set face showed no emotions as he shuffled through the pictures of Derek ladled onto the cold marble splashed with ink and blood.
His eyes narrowed slightly as he picked up a photo of what could only be a harpoon. Blinking slowly in contemplation, Winston accepted this as a clue, however strange, and pocketed the photo.
He pulled out another, a picture of a gang tattoo, and subsequently made his way towards his next suspect.

Arriving at the edge of the harbor, he could smell the salty breeze that carried a strong odor of fish and seaweed. Loosely tethered to the slippery wooden dock with expertly tied knots, the sign of someone familiar with ropes, the fishing vessel stood tall and forbidding, bristling with equipment that included several harpoons. He saw the figure of a woman hauling baskets of fresh catch onto the quayside. Her muscles flexed under the strain, but she moved easily and without breaking a sweat.
"Hailey?" Winston questioned, the name hanging heavy in the air between them.
"That's me," she replied, shooting him a glance, but continuing with her task.
"I see your job keeps you in shape," Winston stated, noting her above-average strength with a subconscious nod.
In response, Hailey shrugged, "It pays, and the work isn't half bad."

Hailey radiated an aura of authority. This was her world, she belonged here and the others respected her. One of her coworkers passed by, tipping his head in acknowledgement towards Hailey, "Evening, sister," he greeted.
Winston noticed the respect she commanded. He also noticed the way her colleagues avoided looking at her—or rather, the tattoo inked to her arm.
Before Winston could enquire further, a family passed by them. A group of kids laughing and shoving at each other, a remote jammed into the hands of Hailey as they settled onto a nearby couch.
"Movie night?" Winston asked and received an affirmative nod from her. "Yeah and nobody likes the movies I pick but it's my house so it's my rules."
Intrigued, Winston glanced at the television. His eyebrows raised slightly as he noted the opening scene of a classic crime thriller.
"They don’t usually complain when they don't have the remote though, do they?" he asked, pointing towards the small device.
Hailey smirked, a recognition sparking in her eyes, "Nah. They know better than that."

Amidst all this, Winston noticed a book beneath the coffee table as he turned to leave. Taking a closer look before departing the apartment, he realized it was "The Psychology of Criminal Minds", a book known for its study on famous serial killers.

Noticing his focus on the book, Hailey nonchalantly yawned, indicating a late-night reading habit and added, "Gets me through the night when I can't sleep. Weird preference for late-night read?" She shrugged as if it were nothing, the faintest spark of defiance reflecting in her steely eyes.
Before Winston could get a word in, a fellow gang member approached Hailey, muttering something about Derek’s latest public speech disrespecting their gang. Her face stiffened.

"We'll deal with it," Hailey said, her voice tightening, her demeanor shifting. She glanced briefly at Winston, quickly reading his inquisitive expression, and added, "It's not good to let people trash talk your family."
With that, she sent Winston on his way, staying behind to discuss amongst her 'family' the disrespect Derek had shown towards them.

As Winston loaded up into his car, his thoughts traveled to her book and her expertise with rope ties. The knots were made by someone who knew their way around a rope, and her job on the fishing vessel could’ve easily taught her that.
With that, Winston drove off into the evening, the crime scene photos shuffling on the passenger seat.

Winston found himself entering the grand synagogue. A revered place of worship that gathered a tight-knit community. The murder of Derek had sent shockwaves through the community, threatening to disrupt the tranquility of the sacred space.

Standing under the magnificent dome, Winston noticed Angela, Derek's grandmother who was a highly respected member of the community. She was absorbed in polishing a large silver key - clearly bestowed only to trusted insiders of the community. She appeared not to notice Winston's arrival.
As Winston made his presence known, Angela seemed startled but quickly masked her emotions.
"My apologies for the intrusion, Ma’am. I am here about Derek," Winston delicately approached the subject.
Even though her face remained neutral, the flinch in her eyes revealed her disturbance. "That's quite alright, detective..." she started, her grip tight around the key.

Winston caught sight of her unusually strong hands and robust arms – strange for an elderly woman in her society. Upon asking, he discovered Angela has been an avid fisherwoman since she was a child and had won many titles at local fishing competitions. Her robustness was plausibly from her fishing background.

Despite her attempt to evade pressing questions, Angela seemed uncomfortable and hastily brought the conversation to her past and future challenges in the fishing competitions with Derek. Her anxiety seemed tied to the challenges Derek brought forward and the atmosphere would tense every time Derek's challenge escalated. Derek really got to Angela, making her feel threatened and pushed at her limits in these competitions.
"I remember Derek grinning over that photo; where he caught you secretly betting against him in the last competition," Winston probed. "He told me he intended to expose you at the upcoming one."

Angela's reaction suggested his words hit a nerve, "You see, Detective... Derek, he...knew something. He found proof of my betrayal. He confronted me about it, claimed he would tell everyone if I didn't stop it. I would lose everything."
Winston registered the shock in his eyes. She had unwittingly given him the most crucial lead. Was this betrayal solely related to the fishing competitions or was there something even more sinister?
As Winston prepared to leave, Angela asked, "Do you think this could have escalated beyond our fishing rivalry? Derek confronting me about the bets and all..."

He chose not to comment, giving Angela an assuring smile before leaving. But the words lingered in his mind long after he left the synagogue. The certainty was that Angela's secret was at risk of exposure. Derek knew, confronted her, had proof, and threatened to share it. Angela felt cornered and threatened - enough to resort to desperate measures?

As he stared pensively at the large synagogue receding in his rear-view mirror, Winston pieced together the web of events and motives pointing at Angela. Derek's death in the synagogue, Angela's robust fishing skills, her betrayal, Derek’s confrontations, the high-stakes competition, the key, and her fear—it seemed like the seemingly kind grandmother Angela was not as innocent as he initially thought.

rounds.evidence_text: In the aftermath of a devastating home explosion that claims the life of Angela, seasoned Detective Winston hones in on two prime suspects: Patrick and Alvin.

Detective Winston grimly regarded the charred remains of Angela's home, considering the pieces of evidence. Home explosions were not commonly dealt with in his line of work, though he knew very well that such explosives were often used in demolitions.

With such knowledge, he was reminded of a local surfing instructor who also took part in an unconventional part-time job that would put him in frequent touch with explosives, training weekly on handling and disposal. This wasn't his usual surfing job but his part-time work as a demolition worker. This was no doubt, Patrick.

Finding his interview notes with Patrick, Winston decided it was time to speak with him again. Winston had known Patrick through his work, not because he surfed but because of his other role in demolition, an occupation that naturally involved a great deal of work with explosives.
Winston set off to the beach in search of Patrick, eventually spotting him as he was patiently teaching a young boy how to ride the waves. "Patrick!" he called out to him.
Recognizing Winston, the man navigated back to shore on his surfboard with a practised ease. "Detective Winston," he greeted, wiping the saltwater off his face. "How can I help you?"

"Just a few questions," Winston replied. He opened his notebook to a page of carefully penned notes about Patrick's financial troubles. "I heard that you've been having some trouble... getting into a failed investment, left with a sizeable debt?”
Patrick's face tightened, but he nodded in admission. "That's right. Lost all my savings, even borrowed a huge amount from Angela, but the investment went under."
"Angela had been lending you money, huh?" Winston asked, wanting to confirm the loan from Angela. "And you haven't been able to pay her back because you lost your main job?"
“That’s correct, detective,” the man answered, his face grim with the weight of his troubles.
"Angela ever threaten to, oh, say, call the police on you?" Winston casually asked, inspecting the worn strap of his watch.
Patrick hesitated before finally sighing and admitting, "Yes, she did. More than once. I guess she had enough of my money problems and empty promises."
Somewhat satisfied, Winston took down the latest confession. Glancing around the beach, he then asked, "You were around Angela's house the evening of the explosion?"
"Detective... it's not far from here, I often pass by when I go home," Patrick replied, his face tense at the questioning.
"Well, nobody else was around her place at that time," Winston mentioned, "Just an interesting fact."
In the awkward silence that followed, Winston then asked about the part that bothered him the most. "You use explosives much with your part-time work and your frequent training, Patrick?"
Patrick seemed to straighten, “I have, yes, in controlled environments and with appropriate permits.” His voice was firm, perhaps a little defensive.
"Right, part of the job, I guess," Winston nodded, closing his notebook. Not another word was spoken between them as he walked away, leaving a nervous Patrick behind.

Winston gave a slow pull from his coffee as he sat across from Alvin, the typically even-tempered delivery man whose vehicle was loaded and ready for his daily route through town. Alvin's calm demeanor had earned him a reputation among the townsfolk as reliable, if not a tad peculiar due to his habit of having his lunch beside graves.

Alvin's reliable routine encompassed the entire town including the cemetery - on today's agenda, he'd be stopping at Angela's to drop off a package. His daily routines had put him on a first-name basis with Angela, as she always made a point to personally welcome him into her home when he arrived with her deliveries.

"So Alvin, any big plans for today?" Winston asked, making casual conversation. "Oh yes," Alvin replied, a spark in his usually placid eyes. "I've just bought a vintage Victorian-era coffin from an auction. Also, I am picking up some decommissioned explosives from a contact in the military. They're for a historical display I'm working on. Can't wait to get both set up in the living room."

This interest didn't surprise Winston. Alvin was known to frequent antique shops, specifically those that boasted a range of mortuary relics. It was odd, sure, but Alvin being odd was one of the few things that gave him character.

"Did you know Angela?" he asked Alvin in a low tone, a hint of suspicion in his voice. Alvin nodded, "Yes. I deliver her packages regularly. Also," he said after a pause, "I was due to deliver a package to her today."

That tidbit of information Winston knew. Angela was home that day to get her package, but she had not been prepared for what the delivery contained. The investigation revealed that the fatal box delivered to Angela's house was filled with explosives, and the only man who Winston knew had any experience with such devices was Alvin.

Alvin’s past in the military gave him the exposure and knowledge about explosives that most people didn't have. It was common knowledge in their tight-knit community where personal histories were difficult to conceal. While this knowledge alone didn’t constitute evidence, it was certainly one fact of many that were swirling around in Winston’s head.

As Alvin got up to leave, Winston gave him a tight smile, "I hope you enjoy setting up your new coffin and your explosives display, Alvin," he said. “Thank you,” Alvin replied, oblivious to any undercurrent in the conversation, his calm demeanor never wavering.
Winston finished his coffee, his mind firmly focused on the explosion that had taken Angela's life, the package that had been delivered, and questions that were begging to be answered.

rounds.evidence_text: In the midst of the arid desert, Jerry's life was brutally extinguished with a lead pipe, and now, it's up to the astute Detective Winston to sift through the sands of deception woven by suspects Maurice and Rex.

The sun was showing no mercy as detective Winston was driving through the arid plains of the desert, to the reported crime scene where Jerry was found murdered. Destination: The flower garden of his suspect, Rex. Winston knew the victim, Jerry, had met him multiple times there, to admire his unique flower arrangements.
As he came to a halt, an array of colors lay before him, stretching as far as his eye could see. Rex was standing there, tending to his flowers.
"Beautiful, aren't they, Detective?" he gestured toward his unique bloomage that surrounded them, small beads of sweat forming on his forehead.
"They truly are," Winston said. "But, I heard that beauty doesn't come easy for you, Rex. And Jerry demanded a hefty sum of money for his silence, didn't he?"

He paused, mulling over something before he responded. "Well, yes. I was actually out here today collecting some native flowers. And yes, Jerry did ask for money. Threatened to inform the authorities about my secret operation, that I had been illegally importing those exotic flowers to make my arrangements unique."
"Jerry liked these flowers, didn't he?" Winston probed.
"Yes, yes, he did. He often came out here, saw my arrangements in the desert. He especially loved the exotic ones I managed to source."
Winston nodded a simple acknowledgement before changing the subject. "Your neighbors, they tell me they often see you cleaning late into the night, through the window."

Rex let out a light chuckle. "Well, running a renowned flower shop has its challenges, detective. My plants, they need to be cared for, and my shop needs to be spotless. It...reflects on my reputation."
Winston had the inkling of a knowing smile, "And you cannot afford to ruin your reputation? Especially since your reputation thrives on your unique selection of flowers."

"No... no, I can't." Rex’s eyes darted anxiously. "You see, I have... a significant amount of debt from importing those exotic flowers. If people found out about my illegal activities, it would ruin me."
Winston took that in as he surveyed Rex's home which was embellished with several security cameras. "Security is a concern?"

"I'm a bit of a... clean freak," Rex confessed, "I tend to keep my lights on until early morning. And, well, the cameras just help me be sure everything's... as they should be."
   
With the sun beating down on his back, Winston nodded, buttoning up his jacket. After he sat in his car, he took one last look at Rex's property. The exotic allure of the place was fascinating, much like the intricacies of the case he was navigating.

With the gravel crunching under his car tires, Winston pulled out from the desert, leaving the solitary florist behind. His work was far from over, but he was starting to pervade deeper into the mystery that swirled around Rex, the florist.
Detective Winston looked out over the desolate desert landscape, it was a place someone could vanish without a trace. Jerry never had a chance.

The local paramedic Maurice was tasked with transporting Jerry across this barren environment. Winston had spoken to Maurice earlier who confirmed his last call had indeed taken him out to the desert with Jerry.

Winston noted that Maurice was physically fit, as his paramedic work often demanded. He was no stranger to exertion, which also brought Winston’s attention to his utility van. Winston had been informed it was spotted in the desert around the time of Jerry’s murder.

Next to the van, Winston found Maurice's usually well-stocked toolkit. A good paramedic was always prepared, but there was an empty slot. It usually housed a lead pipe, a tool that was often used to safely break windows during rescues. He recalled someone mentioning seeing Maurice carrying a lead pipe before the incident took place.

Winston knew that Maurice had been a paramedic for quite some time, dealing often with stressful situations and difficult patients. He had heard whispers about Maurice's practices from other officers. They had been receiving a flurry of complaints about him from past patients.

Back at precinct, he learned more about Maurice's work history. The records clearly showed a pattern, Maurice's unprofessional conduct seemed to worsen over time. His former nurse had reportedly accused him of unethical practices.

Winston also learnt that Jerry was set to testify at Maurice's malpractice trial that was to be held soon. Jerry was the key witness and without him Maurice's future seemed more secure, but Winston dismissed the thought. It's just a fact, what it means was not up to him.

A glance at the clock told him it was time to end his shift. However, there was one last piece of information that seemed pertinent - There were no reports of any other individuals around desert at the time of Jerry's murder. A lonely crime scene was indeed a peculiar one.

As the day ended, Winston decided to revisit Maurice the next day. The facts weren’t lining up, something just didn’t seem right. He had a gut feeling that they were onto something and the truth was close. Just a little closer.

rounds.evidence_text: In the unforgiving desert landscape, Philip's lifeless body was discovered, a nunchaku the ghastly cause of his demise, leaving Detective Winston on a barren hunt, with Jim and Woodrow as his prime suspects.
Winston was stationed in his dusty sedan, parked down the street from a local second-hand shop. The thrift shop had a distinctive sign above its doorway "Woodrow's Antiques & Collectibles".
His destination was not the thrift store though but the old man sitting in the wooden rocking chair on the front porch of the house just behind the store.
Squaring his shoulders, Winston exited his car and approached the man. The old man nodded at his approach. "Mister Woodrow?" Winston asked.
"That I am. And you don't look like a fan of knick-knacks. So I presume you're a detective?"
"Guilty as charged," Winston replied with a light chuckle. "Mind if I ask you a few questions?"

"It's my property, detective. Love the solitude out here. I usually enjoy my peace but, go ahead," Woodrow motioned toward an empty chair opposite him. Winston noticed the hard lines of Woodrow’s arms, the strong muscles present even in his old age.
Winston opened his notebook, "So, you used to teach martial arts?"

Woodrow smiled, "Yes, indeed. For about 40 years. Even collected a few martial arts pieces during my teaching days. Nunchaku among others," he said pointing towards a small wooden room, laden with antiques and relics.
"You still practice?"
"Everyday," Woodrow responded. "Keeps me young."
Winston checked his notes reminiscing, "The police called me after Philip mentioned he was invited here to your desert property. You had a visit from him recently, didn't you?"
Woodrow stiffened at the name. "Yeah, we got together here at my desert property."
Winston lean forward, "Philip... his actions towards the family, they were consistently abusive, weren't they?"

Woodrow sighed heavily, "Yes, that's true. Bad blood doesn't spoil the family, detective. Philip... he made many mistakes, constantly crossing lines. He never even showed an ounce of remorse. It's been difficult, but I love my family dearly and I do everything in my power to protect them," Woodrow explained, a hint of pain in his aged eyes.
Winston nodded, jotting down notes, "Did Philip come alone on his visit?"
"Yeah," Woodrow confirmed. "Needed help with his car, he said. Practically humiliated me in public when it went down. But yeah... he came, and I was here. Alone."
"Well, thank you for your time, Woodrow," Winston closed his notebook, standing up.
"Don't mention it, detective," Woodrow replied, attention already diverted to his karate dummy in the corner of his sizeable yard.

Winston gave Woodrow one last glance and then set off back to his car, leaving Woodrow alone to his solitude. As he pulled away, he glanced in his rearview mirror to see Woodrow had already begun his martial arts practice for the day.

Winston squinted as the sun reflected off the desert's sands, making the sandy terrain that much hotter. As someone familiar with this environment, Jim often frequented the desert for solitude. Winston was investigating the intriguing murder of Philip and was heading to meet up with Jim, a local dockworker and a person of interest along with his co-workers, Joe and Sam.

Upon reaching Jim's dwelling in this arid scape, he noticed an interesting thing; despite living near the dock, Jim had a relatively dry, rougher demeanor, more suited to the desert heat. It was as if he often retreated to the desert for solitude. Joining him were Joe and Sam, each with their own questions to ask.

Joe casually started the conversation, asking Jim about his likes and dislikes. "Any hobbies you particularly enjoy, Jim?"  Jim chose to talk about the latest football match, his eyes oddly detached despite the commentary. Jim was often evasive when speaking about himself. "What about your family, Jim?", Joe continued. Jim responded, as he often does, with "I'd rather not talk about it."

During their coffee break, Sam tried to steer their conversation towards a lighter topic. "Jim," he asked, "what's your favourite film?" Jim masterfully deflected, changing the subject, commenting about the how the weather reminded him of days when he found solitude in the desert. Noticing this, Sam attempted again, asking Jim about his family, only to receive the same brief, vague answer that always followed inquiries about his private life. "I'd rather not talk about it," was Jim's curt response.

Meanwhile, Winston slowly pushed on his investigation. "Where were you on the night of 15th?", Winston asked gently, securing Jim’s response, "Night of the 15th, officer? Well, I had no work scheduled that day." His accent was thick and laced with something Winston couldn't put his finger on.

Probing gently, Winston asked. "What were you doing in the desert then?" Jim curtly responded, as he often did when being questioned, with "I'd rather not talk about it." His walls visibly starting to come up. A few witnesses had even claimed seeing Jim in the desert often in solitude.

Raising the tension, Winston brought up the topic of the document Philip had discovered concerning Jim's illegal operation at the docks, while also gently highlighting that Jim owed Philip a significant debt. Jim finally admitted to being alone with Philip that day in the desert, which he frequented, who had come to confront him about the debt.

On Philip's murder that happened in the desert while he was in solitude, Jim didn't say much, only admitting to being present in the desert that day. Unphased, Winston mentioned how the ledger detailing illegal activities was found with Philip's corpse, briefly catching a flicker of panic on Jim's face.

Returning to his evasive manner, Jim, when asked about the ledger replied with his typical refrain, "I'd rather not talk about it.", only heightening Winston's suspicions. Revelled in the tension of the meeting, Winston picked up his hat, wiped off the sweat, and left Jim with his thoughts, contemplating his next steps in this twisted desert murder. Meanwhile, the unanswered questions proposed by Joe and Sam added an extra layer of mystery to be unraveled.

rounds.evidence_text: In the eerie darkness of the swamp, Gustavo was found lifeless, seemingly killed by a sickle, leaving Detective Winston in a suspenseful game of deceit with two prime suspects, Zelda and Autumn.

Winston rifled through his case notes, lighting a cigarette as he tried to digest the unusual circumstances swirling around Gustavo's murder. No one expects a death in a quiet town like this, especially not in the vicinity of a swamp.

A local bystander, alarmed by the ruckus, had been the one to call the police. By the time the coppers arrived, Zelda was out of control, throwing haymakers left and right in a violent outburst. Still, Gustavo was spotted meeting with Zelda on the day he was killed, traced back to the swamp- an important detail that gave Winston pause.

Always busy with research trips to the swamp as it housed a rich collection of archival items, Zelda rarely fit in. Her eccentricity set her apart from the local swamp residents and provided locals with ample reason to remember her presence, especially on the day of Gustavo's unfortunate demise.

The apparent lack of a connection between Gustavo and Zelda left Winston puzzled. Little did he realise, he was already neck-deep into a mystery which threatened to unravel many secrets in this charming old town. As he thanked the barkeeper and planned his next move, Winston knew the path ahead was laborious, but the thrill of the chase made it all worth it.

Winston pulled his coat closer, squelching through the damp marsh under the weak morning sun. An investigation into the murder of a known gang member, Gustavo was no light task. Later that night, sipping on a cup of lukewarm coffee, Winston ran over the day's findings. Gang feuds, public humiliation, skills with a sickle, an intimate understanding of the marsh...

His job wasn't to arrive at conclusions, but to collect the facts, the facts that would eventually help the force bring Gustavo's murderer to justice. As a detective, his role was, as always, laying down the path for others to tread.

rounds.evidence_text: In the piercing silence of a New York night, Dwayne's life was brutally ended by a sickle's blade in his own car, launching Detective Winston into a dangerous game of truth and lies with suspects, Anthony and Max.

The empty passenger seat next to where Dwayne’s life was taken was a jarring image, the shadow of the uneven coat hanger sticking out like some grotesque sculpture. Only two people on the scene – the deceased and the driver. Max.

Anthony, no stranger to Dwayne's criticism, had requested a meeting with Dwayne. "Dwayne," he had written, "it's urgent. We meet by your car. You know the place." Anthony had the keys to the car belonging to the man he disagreed with most, the man whose disbelief became a source of disdain for him.

Winston remembered the sobering reality --- he now stood at the very location of their meet. Dwayne's car. A discovery that was both alarming and fascinating, considering Anthony was, to his knowledge, the only other person who had access to it.
Back at his office, Winston eyed the order forms, spread wide on his disheveled desk. Sickle after sickle being ordered in retrospect, all intended for Anthony's art projects.

"Why sickles? Isn't it a bit risqué in these times, Anthony?" Winston once asked him. Anthony merely laughed it off, avoiding the question. Today, as he pieced together the facts of Dwayne's demise, the laugh was rather disquieting.

Winston blew out a tired breath, tapping his pen against a stack of papers. This case was becoming a complex labyrinth, and Anthony, once just an artist fueled by his faith, was slowly emerging as a puzzle piece of bewildering proportions.

rounds.evidence_text: In the quiet of a home office, Mackenzie met a fiery end via a flamethrower, leaving Detective Winston tasked with questioning the two unlikely suspects, Sophia and Virgil.

Virgil himself was standing in the front yard, admiring his Adonis-like physique in the car's reflective paint. His obscenely large biceps rippled as he flexed, each one larger than Winston's head.

"Winston, Detective Winston. Can we talk?" Winston called out, causing Virgil to jump and spin around. Upon seeing Winston, a man of authority, Virgil noticeably tensed. His nostrils flaring, Virgil responded, "Alright, Detective. What's this about?"

Winston watched as his gaze flicked back to the Ferrari and began, "I believe you know Mackenzie? You were seen at her house the day she was killed." Virgil's eyes widened a fraction but he quickly composed himself. He admitted, "Yes, I was there. She often asks me to move around some of her heavy furniture in her home office."

"I heard a rumor Mackenzie mocked your achievement in bodybuilding and eventually sold your trophy," Winston added. Virgil bristled at the mention of Mackenzie's name, a flicker of something passing over his face.

"Let's talk inside, feel more comfortable," Virgil said, leading Winston into his house. Virgil's house was immaculate. There was a separate room full of neatly categorized shelves crammed with documentaries and notebooks tagged with the names of the documentaries. The notebooks contained detailed diagrams, timelines and highlights of key events in the documentaries. It confirmed Winston's previous report that Virgil was quite into the True Crime genre.

The most surprising feature in his house was a giant glass case, empty and dust-free. It was obviously a place for something too valued to be manhandled. "That empty spot used to be occupied by my bodybuilding trophy, an achievement that required countless hours in the gym and disciplined nutrition," Virgil said with a hard edge to his voice, "then Mackenzie took it, belittled my effort and sold it."

Winston's gaze flickered between the muscular man and the empty cabinet briefly before responding, "A champion bodybuilder, impressive. I heard about your hardship and dedication. Shame about the trophy, though, they're hard to replace." Virgil's eyes blazed with something akin to anger but he made no comment.

As he was leaving, Winston briefly considered the muscle-bound man. Witnesses who had seen him at Mackenzie's house on the day of the incident... his collection of true crime documentaries... Mackenzie's mockery and theft of his prized bodybuilding trophy. The facts were like an incomplete jigsaw puzzle.

As he studied the video, he noticed Sophia, a recurring figure, found on the grainy footage both at the foot of a local dealer’s four-story warehouse and Mackenzie's home, the same dealer who supplied Mackenzie's esteemed art collection.

“I’ve seen her around,” said Mackenzie’s neighbor on the shaky video clip, which Winston obtained from the CCTV mounted on Mackenzie's front porch. “She was here, at Mackenzie’s house. She comes by now and then to show off her new art pieces.”

During his late-night surveillance, Winston had footage of Sophia transporting flamethrowers into her art studio, an arresting sight, but less so when considering her chosen artistic medium. As dawn broke over the city, Winston observed Sophia's art studio, pinpointing comings and goings. Indeed, Sophia was handling a flamethrower, a tool he learned was frequently featured in her work. Her signature piece was a charred wooden structure, only achievable through the extensive use of a flamethrower.

Contacting Mackenzie, Winston discovered her involvement in Sophia's struggle with substances. Mackenzie confessed to finding Sophia's hidden stash inside her own house during a visit from Sophia. This shocking revelation precipitated her intervention. Mackenzie threatened to sever the financial lifeline she provided for Sophia's art unless Sophia sought recovery. In fact, Mackenzie warned of public disgrace if Sophia didn't get help, wanting the world to know of her addiction unless cured.

Inside Sophia's studio, Winston found sculptures that contained charred elements, hues possible only by the flame's lick. He also discovered stacks of unpaid bills, a barren bank account ledger, and tell-tale drug paraphernalia. This grim scene painted a clear picture of Sophia's financial desperation and her fiendish need for drugs. Not only was her art unique but also for sale. Mackenzie was interested in buying a certain piece - Sophia had agreed to this transaction, as evidenced by Mackenzie's name tacked on one of the art pieces.

Sophia's living arrangements reflected her financial ruin. A note from Mackenzie, garishly displayed on her wall, hinted at the ultimatum over art funds unless Sophia cleaned up her act, a common maneuver in attempts at addiction intervention.

In the sanctuary of Mackenzie's home office, Winston unearthed documents revealing Mackenzie's heavy financial involvement in Sophia's life. Her contributions extended to Sophia's seemingly exorbitant rent, endless supply of canvases, paint, and even the shadowy corners of her addiction - her drugs. Mackenzie was more to Sophia than just a client, she was her de facto financier, the backbone to her irresponsible indulgence.

With this newfound perspective of the complexities of Sophia's life, Winston discovered evidence of newly discovered drug stash tucked away in an unassuming plastic bag marked with Sophia’s initials, found in Mackenzie's office. Sophia’s tangled web of deception began to unravel, but Winston remained composed. His mission was to discover and present the facts, navigating through the labyrinthine maze of lies.

rounds.evidence_text: In the heart of a verdant rainforest, Isla had tragically met her end by a lead pipe, prompting Detective Winston to start sifting through the eerie silence, with Jesse and Brian as the prime suspects.

Winston had barely finished his coffee when he received the call. It was his day off, a rare occasion in the life of a hardened detective, but duty didn't respect quiet mornings or coffee. The unfortunate murder of Isla had occurred on his watch and it was up to him to untangle the clues left behind.

He found himself standing in a vast rainforest. The very place where Isla met her untimely demise. His experienced eyes scanned the area before landing on a familiar figure. It was Brian, the janitor, seen at all hours, obsessively stalking Isla. It was just his luck that he was wiping away the forest's mess on the same day Isla was murdered.
"Brian," Winston nodded in his approach.
"Detective," Brian glanced over, he had the sort of look about him that suggested countless solitary hours, only interrupted by the hustle of cleaning.

"I've been hearing you're no stranger to dealing with broken things." Winston observed Brian's hands that were well-versed in handling tools: hammers, wrenches, even lead pipes. His workspace, a vast and meticulous orchestration of order amidst chaos, was proof of that.

"Mmm, yeah." Brian's face softened. A chase of a memory flickered over his face of all the times he had publicly declared his deep love for Isla. "Isla was one of those broken things. I thought I could fix her. My love her was no secret. I couldn’t live without her,” he confessed his frequent late night contemplations.

Despite the heaviness of the conversation, Winston resumed his careful perusal of Brian’s workspace. His attention was drawn to eerily similar lead pipes, ones that resembled the murder weapon the most. They were common in Brian's line of work, not only for the miscellaneous repairs but also to manage some uncontrollable burst pipes.
"Managed to fix a burst pipe, haven't you Brian?" Winston queried, but pondered, could that skill have escalated to the darker realms?
"Many of them, to be exact. That one over yonder nearly ruined my workspace." Brian chuckled, pointing at a spot behind Winston.
"And yet you're here, hours after word gets out about Isla…”
“It’s been a decade, detective. A decade plus of working in this rainforest and Isla was…” Brian's voice hitched a moment, "...she was everything. I couldn't live without her."

Just then, a soft rustling filled the silence. To Winston's surprise, the lights of Brian's obsession with Isla emerged. He intuitively directed Winston five steps to the left. A moment later, a large tree branch came crashing down exactly where Winston had stood, a product of the lush, unpredictable rainforest Brian had been maintaining for over a decade.
"Thanks. I suppose you know this place, like back of your hand, huh?"
"Yeah. Comes with the territory."

Winston repeated his mantra mentally. Every suspect is just a character until proven guilty. As he wound his way back, the very last thing his purposeful steps echoed in Brian's lonely world was when Isla’s public rejection had embarrassingly stung Brian.

But facts were facts. A man, admittedly obsessed with a woman, now found murdered in a place he had called home for a decade, at a time he definitely was present. A man who liked to fix things, had access to tools, especially lead pipes. All facts, all cataloged. But Winston was far from writing the end to this chapter. As the detective stalked off, his mind was already moving, spinning, weaving another part of this tragic story.

Winston was alert to the rustling sounds of the rainforest, conscious that this deceptively peaceful location hid a sinister secret. A murder had taken place here and Isla, a devoted member of a local club for enthusiasts of unsolved crimes, was the victim. Her lifeless body, found under a fallen tree, and a near-by lead pipe marked the tragic remnants of an unsolved crime. Winston was compelled to uncover the truth, especially as he was cognizant of a deep, dark secret that Isla had discovered: Jesse, the president of their club, was involved in illegal activities.

Jesse's name was constantly mentioned during the initial investigations. He was no ordinary member of the club, he was the president and also a famed drummer. His rhythmic skills had not only provided him with a lifestyle most would envy but also a sizable disposable income, leading to his immense respect and love from his community. Jesse was known for having a lot of free time, especially on the weekends. Jesse became Winston's next stop in the investigation.

Ignoring the pulsating heat of the afternoon, Winston headed to Jesse's house. Guided by the rhythmic sounds of a drum that echoed in the stillness, he made his way. As he neared, the drumming ceased and Jesse's piercing gaze met him.
"Detective Winston," Jesse rose to his feet, "I've been expecting you."
"Expecting me?" Winston asked, a raised eyebrow almost disappearing under his cap.
"Yes, I heard about poor Isla," Jesse replied, a flicker of sadness crossed his face.

Jesse was a frequent visitor of the rainforest during his free weekends, a place he went seeking inspiration for his musical compositions. "Rainforest vibes, man, they produce the best drum solos," he said, crediting his most impressive works as a drummer to the time he spent in the rainforest, jotting down notes in his notepad.
Suddenly, his phone rang and he seemingly needed privacy for the call, returning after a few minutes looking flustered. Winston noted this change but didn't comment.

Jesse began to discuss the club. He described it as a casual group that met every fortnight to discuss famous unsolved crime mysteries, watch documentaries, and talk about criminal profiling. "The irony," he laughed dryly, "now we have our own club mystery."

Talking about Isla seemed to disturb him. He confessed, "I overheard Isla a few days ago... she found out about my… my involvement in illegal activities. She was planning to go to the police…” Jesse was visibly worried, afraid that this could potentially shatter his career, and with it, his sizable disposable income and tarnish his reputation.
Silently pondering the possibility of Jesse having been pushed to silence Isla, Winston finished his coffee, neatly recording the conversation in his mind’s eye for later.

Pulling on his coat, Winston was enveloped again by the rainforest’s familiar sounds. His clear blue eyes squinting determinedly into the shifting shadows. He knew that the next chapter of this twisted tale was yet to be penned, but he was one step closer now, the connection between Isla's exposure of Jesse’s illicit activities and her untimely death seemed more likely.

"Yes, sir," Jose replied quietly. "The man even suspects me for the murder that happened here last week, during my shift. If Terry fires me... everything comes crashing down. This is the main work I've got right now... I can't afford to lose it."
Winston nodded understandingly and asked him if Terry, who was also present during the murder event, was around the vineyard at this time, to which Jose confirmed.

A scenario that happened right after Terry caught Bella red-handed with a bottle of rare, expensive wine she hadn't paid for. An intern. Bella, whose name had been brought up more and more frequently in recent times due to her increasing thieving activities.

"Ma'am," Winston began. His greeting was met with a simple nod from Bella.
"Bella, correct?"
"Yes, Sir," she replied.
"You were here all day?"
She nodded. "Everyone around here can tell you that," she murmured.

An old red-and-green painted shed stood in the distance. He knew Bella had the privilege of going in and out without supervision. A luxury that troubled him, especially given her recent knack for stealing.
"Busy day today?" Winston asked, glancing at Bella's hands.
"Always. I keep these tools as clean and sharp as possible," she replied, holding up a newly sharpened pruner. Her delicate hands belied the hardened steel of the instruments.
Winston nodded, casting his gaze to one of the metal figurines intricately sculpted by Bella herself.
"You do this?" he asked, pointing.

Bella nodded, a small smile flashing across her face. She seemed to relish the precision, the skill required, and the metalwork. It was clear she was good at this. His eyes narrowed slightly as he put the figurine back down.

Her penchant for stealing wasn't just limited to the tools or anything she could lay her hands on. It was whispered around the vineyard that Bella had a keen taste for the wine here. Especially the rare and pricey varieties, which had been disappearing more frequently than before. Terry wasn't a fan though, especially after catching her in the act. Winston had found himself unusually bothered by what was open knowledge. Particularly, Terry's threat to report Bella to management if it continued.

On his way back to his cruiser, Winston remembered a particularly vivid memory from his briefing; Terry shouting at Bella right in front of the shed. The memory sent a chill running down his spine. He wore a stoic face in front of her, nodded in acknowledgment, and walked away. His gut was telling him that she had more to say, and he planned to stick around. Somewhat of a sixth sense, he attributed it to his years on the force.

rounds.evidence_text: In the neon glow of a laser tag arena, Jacqueline's life is abruptly ended by snake venom, leaving Detective Winston with two suspects - Abigail and Veronica - and a most unusual murder mystery to solve.

Winston sifted through scraps of evidence, photos, and notes strewn across his desk. Jacqueline, a big fan of a certain singer, Veronica, was his latest case, a priority due to the unusual circumstances surrounding her death - snake venom, of all things, at a laser tag arena concert, no less. A concert that shockingly happened to be on the very day of her murder.
A flier of Veronica's concert caught his eye, purple lasers splashed across the front. It had been widely promoted online - Veronica herself had announced it on her social media accounts.

Veronica's social media had been a hotbed of activity ever since she had publicly insulted Jacqueline's nationality during a recent performance, causing several heated public altercations both online and at the arena due to this prejudice. It caused quite the stir on the internet.
Remembering the online fuss, Winston did some digging and arranged a meeting with Veronica via her manager.
"Hello Detective, how can I help you?", Veronica asked. Her songwriter's pen was twirling between her fingers absentmindedly.
"I'm on the Jacqueline case", Winston answered stoically.
A flicker of emotion crossed Veronica's face, "I remember her...We had an argument at a party...about our nationalities." She avoided Winston's gaze.
"Hmm, those racial tensions caused quite a frenzy both at your shows and on social media. Is that correct?" Winston pointedly asked. Veronica’s mouth twisted, but she said nothing.
Winston changed course, "You used to work at a snake farm, isn't that right?"
"Yes,” Veronica replied nervously. “It was indeed, and would you imagine the irony, where I performed a week before Jacqueline's murder. They called later saying some venomous snake was missing."
"Interesting," muttered Winston. "You also penned a research paper about snake venoms, is that right?"
Veronica looked genuinely surprised, "Yes, how did you know?"
"I find it important to know about people I'm investigating. I also know that Jacqueline was a big fan of your music."

With that, he wrapped up the interview, leaving Veronica a little perplexed. Back at the precinct, he sifted through the scattered notes and typed up his report. Nothing was solved yet, but the pieces were moving into their respective slots.

Detective Winston flipped through the dossier. The laser tag arena was usually a place of fun, but now it was marked by tragedy -- Jacqueline's death. Abigail was the last person in the room with Jacqueline. She had been there volunteering for a charity event, with Jacqueline's team participating in the event. The severity of the situation felt at odds with the colorful neon lights illuminating the fluorescent walls and synthetic turf.

He walked into the arena, noting the silence that hung in the air. He recalled the fact that the owner could hardly give him any insight given that he was preoccupied at his convenience store during the night shift. Winston checked the store's transaction records, Abigail had indeed been here in the laser tag arena, her payment indicated her presence. Abigail had also been involved with the reptile exhibit at the local zoo; he was also informed of a recently attended seminar on venom extraction. That little detail felt oddly chilling in the context of the events.

Abigail's neighbor, when questioned, told him about his nocturnal TV watching pastime. His enjoyment of late-night soap operas inadvertently gave him a clear view of her door, consistently noting Abigail's comings and goings, her odd hours, and her solitary existence.

He took a trip down to the zoo. It was awash with excited children and worn-out parents. A small sign heralded the reptile house as of particular interest, with potent venom snakes prolifically cited. A zookeeper mentioned a few offhanded comments Abigail had made about how venom extraction wasn't so difficult, it gave Winston pause.

As he left, the shocking reality hit him - notably one fact, no one else had entered the laser tag room at the time of the event. Abigail and Jacqueline were the only two in the room. There was still more to be done, more evidence to be collected.
"Where were you when Jacqueline was bitten by a snake, Abigail?" He asked in his careful detective's tone. Abigail laughed nervously, her eyes darted around before landing on him again.
"I've told you, I was in the main lobby." She replied, folding her arms protectively over her chest. "Look, detective, I work at a zoo. The reptiles are my job, not some kind of hobby, okay?"

They had wrapped up their conversation, and he was left with some threads of information that were yet to be woven into a full picture. It was time to follow the clues, to unravel the tightly woven mystery around the tragic end of Jacqueline.

rounds.evidence_text: In the glitz and glamour of a bustling casino, a deadly secret unfolds as Iris is found lifeless by a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with two puzzling suspects - Madison and Christine.

Her worn-out van had become a makeshift storage space for building equipment. Winston couldn't help but notice the glow from a lead pipe resting within the remaining pile. The pipe surreptitiously nestled between hammer and screwdriver.

Iris' testimony, scheduled to be presented at the court soon, had been against Madison's illegal shenanigans. Layers of intrigue were folded over the delicate connection: the lawyer had informed Madison about her upcoming ordeal. Such update from Madison's lawyer would often coincide with the time she saw Iris leaving for her customary Friday night casino visits. The irony of it burnt brighter than the burgeoning dawn.

Following a trail of circumstantial evidence, Winston discovered that Madison had been threatened with eviction due to her illicit affairs. The threat had surely hanged like a smog around her, dark and ominous.

Frequent visits to the casino by Iris could be seen as just a pastime or, to a mind uncertain of the future, as potential avenues for threat mitigation. Madison's observations of Iris's Friday night gambles could be a coincidence... or a clear implication of premeditation.

Casino surveillance tapes confirmed the regular presence. Madison and Iris, both regular features under the glaring camera lights. The unblinking eye of the casino camera had captured Madison's presence around the vicinity even as the clock chimed Iris's hour of departure from the world.

Winston found himself standing before the courthouse doors, a paper with fresh ink in his hands. Iris had been there, holding the very same documents, their legality meant to condemn Madison in a court of law.

Casual yet conspicuous, Madison had been seen overhearing the constant chatter of Iris about her late-night casino visits. Her lawyer's advice combined with the threat of eviction added fuel to the tension... Winston sighed deeply as he shielded the court documents from the continual rain.

Piecing together the jigsaw puzzle seemed daunting. Again, his thoughts revolved around Madison under her hard hat. His next steps unraveling her story had all begun with Iris' murder. Now it was only an endless chase after blurry silhouettes of half-truths. Only time would tell how Madison fits into all of this.

"Just following up on some loose ends," he replied, his gaze trained on the computer she just closed and the designs she was now carrying in her arms. He asked to see them.
